- Measuring and quantifying structures consistently, such as sizing a finding or calculating a volume.
- Assisting with screening programmes in specific, well studied settings.

A clearance means a regulator reviewed evidence for a stated intended use. It does not mean the tool is right for every patient population, scanner or hospital. Read the intended use statement. It is usually narrower than the marketing.

## What is less certain

Several gaps recur, and they deserve scepticism.

**Performance on different populations and equipment.** A model trained on images from a few hospitals can lose accuracy when it meets different scanners, protocols or patient demographics. This is often called a generalisation problem. A strong result at the developer's site is a starting point, not proof for yours.

**Retrospective versus real world results.** Many studies test a model on past, curated images. Real clinics bring poor quality scans, unusual cases and time pressure. Prospective studies that follow outcomes in live practice are harder, slower and rarer, and they matter more.

**Accuracy versus benefit.** A tool can detect a finding accurately and still fail to improve care. Finding more small abnormalities may lead to more follow up tests without changing outcomes. Evidence on patient benefit, not only detection rates, is what to look for.

**Human and machine together.** How a radiologist responds to an AI suggestion is a research subject in itself. Automation bias, where people over trust a prompt, and the reverse, where they ignore it, both appear. The combined system's performance is what counts.

**Drift over time.** Equipment gets upgraded, protocols change and disease patterns shift. A model that performed well at purchase can degrade quietly without monitoring.

## Questions to ask a vendor

If you are evaluating a product, a plain set of questions cuts through a great deal.

- What exact task and population is it cleared or validated for?
- Was it tested on data from sites unlike the ones it was built on, and was that data kept separate from training?
- Is there evidence from live clinical use, and has it been published or independently reviewed?
- How does it perform for subgroups, and where does it do worst?
- What happens on the cases it gets wrong, and how are those surfaced?
- How is performance monitored after installation?

A serious vendor will answer these directly and admit limits. Evasion is information too.

## The operational side

Much of the real work is not the model. It is integration. Images flow from scanners through a PACS, results must return to the reporting workflow, and the output must appear where the clinician is already working. A tool that needs a separate login and a separate screen tends to be ignored.

Plan for standards based integration with existing systems rather than bespoke connections. Make the interface show clearly what the AI did and did not assess, so no one assumes more than was done. Keep an audit trail recording which version of the model produced which output, because a model update changes behaviour and you will want to know which version read which scan. Give clinicians a route to report errors, and make sure someone acts on those reports.

Data governance needs its own attention: where images are processed, what leaves the hospital, and on what legal basis. Imaging data is sensitive health data under laws such as the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 and GDPR, and a vendor that processes it in the cloud is a processor you must be able to account for.

Staffing matters too. Someone has to own the tool after the launch meeting: reviewing the error reports, talking to the vendor about updates, and deciding when to switch it off. Without a named owner, even a good tool decays into an ignored banner on a screen.

### Context in lower resource settings

Imaging AI is sometimes proposed as a way to extend scarce specialist capacity, where radiologists are few and distances are long. The motivation is understandable. The cautions apply with extra force: image quality varies, equipment may differ from what the model learned on, and follow up care must exist for anything the tool flags. A finding with no pathway to treatment is not an improvement. Local validation matters more, not less, and so does training for the staff who will see the output.

## A measured approach

Caution here is not hostility to the technology. It is how useful tools earn trust.

Start with a narrow, well defined use such as worklist prioritisation, where the AI changes order rather than diagnosis. Run it in shadow mode first, where it produces outputs that are compared to clinicians' decisions without influencing them. Review the results with the clinicians who will use it. Then expand only as the local evidence supports it.

The honest summary is that AI in imaging is real, useful in specific roles and often unproven beyond them. Treat each claim as a question about a particular task, population and workflow, and ask for the evidence that fits your own.

title: Onboarding Is a Saga, Not a Form
excerpt: Provisioning a customer touches five systems and can fail in the middle of any of them. Treating it as a durable transaction is the difference between a stalled signup and a support ticket.
author: Altisly Engineering
content:
## What actually happens when somebody signs up

On paper it is one action. In practice, approving a tenant means creating a schema, running every migration against it, seeding catalogues and defaults, writing the subscription and its entitlements, applying branding, creating the first administrator, sending an invitation, and recording that all of it happened.

That is eight things, across at least three systems, any of which can fail. The interesting question is not how to make them succeed. It is what the system looks like when number six fails at three in the morning.

## The version everybody builds first

The first version is a request handler. It does the eight things in order, wrapped in whatever transaction it can reach, and returns success.

When step six fails, you get a tenant that exists in the database, has a schema, has no administrator, and cannot be signed into. The customer has been told they are approved. Nobody on your side knows the state is broken until they write in. The fix is an engineer with a database console and a good memory.

And the retry is worse than the failure. Run it again and you have two subscription rows, or a second invitation, or a migration applied twice.

## Making it durable

We rebuilt provisioning as a saga. Each step is recorded before it runs and marked when it completes. The whole thing is resumable, and every step is idempotent: running it twice produces the same state as running it once.

That changes the failure conversation entirely. Step six failing at three in the morning is now a row that says step six failed at three in the morning. The run resumes from there, either automatically or when an operator presses a button, and it does not redo the five steps that already landed.

Two axes matter here. What the tenant is (their lifecycle state) and how far provisioning has got (the run state) are different facts, and conflating them is how you end up with a tenant that looks active and is not usable.

## Idempotency is the real work

Most of the effort is not the state machine. It is making each step safe to repeat.

Creating a schema becomes create if absent. Seeding becomes upsert against a stable key. Sending an invitation becomes send unless one is already outstanding, which means invitations need identity of their own rather than being a side effect. Every one of those is a small design decision that only looks necessary once you have accepted that steps will be retried.

## What it gives back

Operators stop being a recovery mechanism. When something stalls, the platform surface shows exactly which step, with the error, and a resume that is safe to press.

Support conversations change shape. Instead of asking a customer to describe symptoms, you look at the run.

And the customer experience holds. Onboarding either completes or resumes. It does not silently strand somebody in a half created workspace with a login that does not work.

## The wider point

Any process that crosses more than two systems and gets triggered by a human decision deserves this treatment. Approvals. Cancellations. Bulk imports. Anywhere the middle of the process is a real place a system can be, the middle needs to be a state you can see and act on, not an accident.

title: The Hidden Cost of Microservices for Small Teams
excerpt: A six person team does not have the coordination problem microservices solve, but it pays every cost. Why we usually recommend a modular monolith, and when splitting does make sense.
author: Altisly Strategy Team
content:
A team of six engineers decides to build their new product as eight services. The reasoning is familiar: it will scale, teams can work independently, and it is how the large companies do it. Eighteen months later, two of those engineers spend most of their week on deployment pipelines and a third is permanently debugging why the order service and the billing service disagree.

Nothing went wrong in any dramatic way. The team simply paid a set of costs that were designed for organisations ten times their size.

## What microservices are actually for

Microservices solve an organisational problem more than a technical one. When a hundred engineers share one codebase, they block each other: merges collide, releases queue and one team's bug takes down another's feature. Splitting into services lets groups ship on their own schedule.

That benefit scales with the number of people. For a team of five to fifteen, the coordination problem it solves barely exists. You can talk to each other. You can agree on a release. The cost, however, arrives in full from day one.

## The costs nobody puts in the plan

**Every call becomes a network call.** Inside a single application, calling a function is nearly free and nearly always works. Between services, the call can time out, fail halfway or arrive twice. Each boundary needs timeouts, retries, idempotency and a decision about what to do when the other side is down. That is real design work, repeated for every pair of services that talk.

**Transactions disappear.** In one database, you can update an order and a payment together and have both succeed or both fail. Across two services with two databases, you cannot. You need sagas, compensating actions and reconciliation jobs. These are solvable problems, and they are also a good deal harder than a database transaction.

**Debugging gets slower.** A single request now touches five services. To see what happened you need distributed tracing, consistent correlation IDs and logs you can search across all of them. Without those, you are guessing. With them, you have built and must maintain an observability stack.

**Deployment multiplies.** Eight services means eight pipelines, eight sets of configuration, eight runtime environments and versioning between them. A change that spans two services needs coordinated releases or careful backwards compatibility. Many small teams discover they have built a platform team's workload without a platform team.

**Local development degrades.** Running the whole system on a laptop becomes a project. New joiners lose days to setup. Tests that need several services are slow and brittle, so people stop running them.

**Data gets duplicated.** Services own their data, so anything shared is copied or fetched. Copies drift. Teams then spend time deciding which copy is authoritative.

### The cost that compounds

These costs are individually manageable. The trouble is that they compete with the product for the same few people. Each hour spent on service mesh configuration or contract versioning is an hour not spent on the thing customers pay for.

Hiring is affected as well. A small team that runs many services needs people who are comfortable with containers, orchestration, networking and tracing as well as the product code. Those people are scarce and expensive, and a team that cannot hire them ends up with operational knowledge held by one or two individuals. When one of them goes on leave, the system becomes a risk nobody else can assess.

Cloud bills grow quietly too. Each service carries its own baseline of compute, its own database instance and its own share of monitoring and logging. Eight small services running all day rarely cost less than one application doing the same work, and the difference is paid for before a single customer arrives.

And the boundaries themselves are guesses. Early in a product, you do not know where the natural seams are. Draw them wrongly and you get a distributed monolith: services that cannot change independently, that must deploy together, and that share a database through the back door. You have all the cost of microservices and none of the benefit.

## What we prefer

For most small teams, we recommend a well structured single deployable, often called a modular monolith. One codebase, one deployment, one database, with clear internal modules and strict rules about how they interact.

The discipline is in the boundaries. Each module exposes a small interface and hides its tables. Other modules call the interface, never reach into the data. Dependencies point in one direction. You can enforce this with tooling and code review.

Picture a lending product with modules for customers, loans, repayments and notifications. In a modular monolith, the repayments module asks the loans module for a balance through a defined function. In a service design, the same question is a network request with retries and failure handling. The business logic is identical. Only the second version needs a second deployment, a second database and an on call rota.

This gives you most of the architectural clarity of services with none of the network. And it keeps your options open. A module with a clean boundary can be extracted into its own service later, when you know it needs one.

## When splitting does make sense

We are not against services. There are good reasons to split:

- A component has a genuinely different scaling profile, such as an image processing worker that needs many cheap machines.
- It needs a different technology, security boundary or compliance scope. Isolating payment card handling is a common example.
- A part of the system has a separate team that owns it end to end and wants a separate release cadence.
- Its failure must not take down the rest, and isolation is the cheapest way to guarantee that.

Notice that each reason is specific and observable. "We might need to scale" is not on the list.

## A test before you split

Ask these questions about any proposed service. Can one person explain what it owns in a sentence? Does it have its own data that nobody else needs to write? Could it be down for an hour without stopping the core product? Would a separate team really run it? If the answers are mostly no, keep it as a module.

## Start simple, stay honest

Write the decision down with the reasons, so the next person can tell whether those reasons still hold.

The best sign that you are ready for services is that you can name the specific pain. A deploy that blocks two teams every week, a component that needs ten times the machines of everything else, a compliance boundary an auditor keeps asking about. Pain you can name justifies a split. Pain you only imagine rarely does.

Revisit the decision as the team and product grow. The right architecture for six engineers is rarely the right one for sixty. The mistake is not choosing services or a monolith, it is borrowing a decision made for someone else's size. Build the simplest thing that your actual team can run well at two in the morning, and split when the pain is real and named.

title: Where Large Language Models Earn Their Keep in Operations
excerpt: Language models are strong at reading messy text and weak at exact decisions. We map where they pay off in operations, where they disappoint, and how to design for their mistakes.
author: Altisly Studio
content:
Ask five operations leads where AI should go in their business and you will get five answers, most of them a chatbot. Ask which tasks in their week are tedious, repetitive and involve reading messy text, and the answers get much more useful. Large language models are good at that second category. They are much weaker at the first.

Our view, after building workflow automation around them and watching where it holds up in practice, is that language models earn their keep in a narrow band of operational work. Outside that band they cost more than they return.

## The shape of a good fit

A language model is, at its core, very good at turning unstructured language into structured output and back. That is the useful part. Operations is full of unstructured language: emails, invoices as PDFs, support messages, free text notes, supplier replies, policy documents.

The best fits share a pattern:

- The input is text or a document with no fixed format.
- A person currently reads it and types the result somewhere.
- A wrong answer is catchable, by a person or by a rule, before it does harm.
- The volume is high enough that the reading time adds up.

When all four hold, a model can take over the reading and leave the deciding to humans and rules.

## Where it works well

**Extraction.** Pull the supplier name, invoice number, amount, currency and due date from a document that arrives in twenty different layouts. Traditional templates break when a supplier changes their format. A model reads the page the way a clerk would. You still validate the result, for example by checking that line items add to the total, but the tedious part is gone.

**Classification and routing.** Read an incoming message and decide whether it is a billing question, a complaint, a request to change details or spam, then send it to the right queue. The model does not resolve anything. It sorts, which is where time is usually lost.

**Drafting.** Write a first reply to a routine query, using your own policies and the customer's record, for a person to review and send. The human edit is the control. This tends to save time even when the draft needs changes, because starting from a draft is faster than starting blank.

**Summarising.** Condense a long ticket history or a thread of forty emails so the next person can act without reading everything. Useful, with the caveat that summaries can omit a crucial detail, so keep the source one click away.

**Search over your own documents.** Answer questions from your policies, contracts and procedures, with references to the passage used. This works when the answer exists in your material and the system is built to cite it.

## Where it disappoints

**Arithmetic and exact lookups.** Models can produce a confident wrong sum. If a number matters, compute it with code and use the model only to read the inputs.

**Decisions with consequences and no check.** Approving a payment, changing a bank account, or granting access should not be a model's call alone. Use it to prepare the case, and let a rule or person decide.

**Anything needing guaranteed consistency.** The same input can produce slightly different outputs. If you need identical results every time, or an audit trail of exact logic, plain code is the right tool.

**Poorly defined processes.** If your team cannot explain how a task is done, a model will not fix that. It will automate the confusion at speed.

## Design for being wrong

A model will occasionally be wrong with complete confidence. That is not a flaw to wait out, it is a property to design around. Practical habits that help:

- Ask for structured output and validate it against a schema. Reject anything malformed.
- Add checks that do not depend on the model, such as totals matching or a supplier existing in your records.
- Route low confidence or failed checks to a person, with the original document beside the model's reading.
- Log inputs, outputs and the human's final answer. That record is how you measure accuracy honestly.

Nobody should have to trust the model blindly, and nobody should have to recheck everything. The goal is not zero errors. It is that errors are caught cheaply, before they reach a customer or a ledger.

## Measure before you scale

Start with a small, real sample. Take a few hundred past cases where you already know the correct result, run them through, and count how often the output is right. Do this before you build anything large. Then keep measuring in production, because documents, suppliers and customer behaviour change.

Be honest about the comparison too. The baseline is not perfection, it is the current process, which includes tired humans making typos. Sometimes a model with review beats the status quo comfortably. Sometimes it does not, and the saving is smaller than the pilot suggested.

### Data and privacy

Operational text often contains personal and financial data. Before sending it to any model provider, know where it goes, whether it is retained or used for training, and what your obligations are under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, GDPR or your sector's rules. Minimise what you send. Strip identifiers that the task does not need. Treat this as a design constraint from the first day, not a review at the end.

## A sensible first project

Pick one high volume, text heavy, low risk task. Inbound document handling or support triage are common candidates. Build it so a person reviews every output at first, measure accuracy, and relax review only where the numbers justify it. If it works, you have a template. If it does not, you have spent weeks, not quarters, finding out.

Language models are not a strategy. They are a capable tool for reading and writing, and the operations that benefit are the ones that know exactly which reading and writing they would like to stop doing by hand.

title: What We Refused to Automate
excerpt: The value in treasury automation was never the model. It was getting the exclusion rules and column mappings out of one person's head and into an artefact.
author: Altisly Strategy Team
content:
## The desk before

A treasury analyst opens seven bank portals, downloads seven files in five formats, and reconciles them against the blotter. Two hours, every morning, before anyone can say what the position is.

The obvious move is to automate the download and the match. That part is mechanical, and it is the part every vendor demonstrates.

The part that matters is underneath it. When the analyst finds a line that does not match, they know that this counterparty books value date one day late, that this account posts fees separately, and that anything under a certain size from that corridor is a rounding artefact and should be excluded. None of that is written down. It is judgement, held by one person, and it is the actual product.

## Encoding judgement, not replacing it

So the first thing we built was not a matching engine. It was a place to put the rules.

Column mappings per source, because every bank exports differently and the mapping is knowledge, not configuration. Exclusion rules with a reason attached, because a rule without its reason is unmaintainable within a quarter. Tolerance bands per corridor. Value date adjustments per counterparty.

Once those existed as an artefact, the matching engine was almost boring to write. It is a loop over rules somebody deliberately stated.

## Where we stopped

We did not automate the decision to break a match. A line that fails every rule surfaces to a human with the full trail: what was compared, which rule excluded what, why the engine could not close it. The human decides.

We did not let a model infer the rules from history. It could probably approximate them. But an approximated rule cannot be defended to an auditor, and cannot be corrected by the analyst who knows the real one. A rule you cannot read is a rule you cannot own.

We did not automate the sign off. Somebody puts their name on the position each morning. That is not inefficiency, that is accountability, and removing it would have made the system worse while making the demo better.

## What actually changed

The two hours became about fifteen minutes, most of it spent on the handful of lines that genuinely need a person.

But the outcome that mattered more was this. When the analyst took two weeks of leave, the desk kept running. Not because a model had learned to be them, but because the thing that lived only in their head was now a file in a repository, reviewed like anything else, with the reasoning attached.

## The rule we now apply

Before automating any operational process, ask where the judgement lives. If it lives in a person, the first deliverable is the artefact that holds it, not the engine that runs it.

Automation applied to undocumented judgement just moves the fragility somewhere harder to see.

title: Offline First Clinical Software for Unreliable Networks
excerpt: When the connection drops at the bedside, software should keep working. We cover local storage, conflict rules, duplicate patients and sync design for clinics with unreliable networks.
author: Altisly Engineering
content:
## The ward does not care about your uptime

A nurse is recording observations at the bedside when the clinic's connection drops. The tablet shows a spinner. Either she waits, or she writes the numbers on her hand and enters them later. Neither is acceptable, and the second is how errors get into records.

Many hospital and clinic systems are designed as if the network were a utility that is always on. In much of Nigeria, Ghana and the wider region, connectivity can be patchy inside the building, slow at peak hours, or absent at a satellite clinic. Software for that setting has to treat the network as a convenience, not a dependency. That is what offline first means.

This piece covers the engineering side only: how to design clinical and operational software so it keeps working when the connection does not. It is not guidance on clinical practice.

## What offline first really means

It is not "has a cache". It means the application is fully usable with no connection, and synchronisation is a background process that happens when it can.

The local device is where work is done. The server is where work is shared. Reads and writes go to local storage first, so the interface is always fast and never blocked on the network. A sync engine then moves changes both ways when a path exists.

This inverts the usual design. In a typical web app the server is the truth and the client is a view. In an offline first app, each device holds a working copy, and the job becomes reconciling copies.

## Decide what must work offline

You cannot make everything offline capable, and trying will bloat the project. List the tasks that a person must complete with no network, in rough priority:

- Registering or finding a patient.
- Recording observations, notes and orders.
- Viewing a recent summary of the patient's record.
- Capturing a dispensing or billing event.

Features that need the wider system, such as a national lookup or an external payment gateway, can degrade gracefully with a clear message and a queued retry. Be explicit about which is which. Users forgive a feature that says "this will send when you are back online". They do not forgive silent loss.

### Local storage and what goes on the device

Records need a durable local store. On the web this is typically IndexedDB, on mobile an embedded database such as SQLite. Either way, data on the device is a security concern, because tablets get lost.

Encrypt local data at rest, require a screen lock or a login, and limit what is stored to what that user's role and assigned patients need. A ward tablet does not need the whole hospital's records. Provide a way to wipe a device remotely or on repeated failed logins, and expire cached data that has not been used for a set period.

## The hard part: conflicts

Two people can edit the same record while apart. A doctor updates a medication list on one device while a pharmacist annotates it on another. When both sync, which version wins?

There is no universal answer, so design by data type.

**Append only data** is the easy case. Observations, notes and events are things that happened. Store them as new entries with a timestamp and author, and never overwrite. Two nurses recording readings at different times do not conflict. They simply both exist.

**Fields that one person owns at a time** can use last write wins, if the loss of the older value is acceptable and visible. Be careful here, because device clocks drift. Prefer a server assigned sequence or a logical clock over trusting the tablet's time.

**Structured, safety relevant data** such as allergies or active medications should not silently merge. When two edits collide, flag it and ask a human to resolve it. A clear "these two changes disagree" screen is safer than a clever algorithm.

Whatever you pick, keep the full history. If a merge decision turns out wrong, you want to see both versions and who made each.

### Identity and duplicates

Offline registration creates a classic problem. Two clinics each register the same patient on the same day, with slightly different spellings. When they sync, there are two records for one person.

Generate record identifiers on the device, using globally unique IDs, so nothing collides on sync. Then treat duplicate detection as a separate, deliberate process: match on a combination of fields, present likely duplicates to staff, and provide a proper merge that keeps an audit trail of what was joined. Avoid automatic merging of clinical records without review.

## Sync design that survives bad networks

The network you are designing for is not simply offline. It is flaky: connections that open and die, requests that time out halfway, uploads that arrive twice.

A few principles help.

- Make every write idempotent. Give each change a unique ID so the server can safely receive it twice.
- Sync in small batches with resumable progress, so a dropped connection loses seconds, not an hour.
- Send changes, not whole records, where possible, to respect limited bandwidth and mobile data costs.
- Keep a visible queue on the device. Staff should be able to see how many changes are waiting and when the last sync succeeded.
- Order matters. Apply changes with their dependencies, so an order does not arrive before the patient it refers to.

### Make the state obvious

Offline systems fail socially when people cannot tell what state they are in. Show a plain indicator of connection and sync status. Mark records that have local changes not yet sent. When sync fails repeatedly, tell the user and say what to do.

### Test the bad days

The failure modes only appear under bad conditions, so test there. Switch the network off mid sync. Edit the same record on two devices. Let a tablet sit offline for a week and reconnect. Corrupt a queued message. These tests are tedious, and they are where offline first systems are won or lost.

## Where to start

If you are building or buying clinical software for unreliable connectivity, begin with one workflow, such as bedside observations or patient registration. Make it work fully offline, with clear conflict rules and a visible sync queue. Prove it in a real clinic with real interruptions, then extend the pattern. Offline first is a discipline of assumptions, and the first assumption to drop is that the network will be there.

title: Reading Postgres EXPLAIN Without Fear
excerpt: Query plans look hostile until you know a handful of terms. A practical guide to reading EXPLAIN output, spotting bad estimates and fixing slow queries without guessing.
author: Altisly Engineering
content:
A query that ran in forty milliseconds last month now takes eleven seconds. Someone pastes a wall of indented text into the chat, with arrows, costs and words like "Hash Right Join", and the room goes quiet. EXPLAIN output looks like it was written for the database, not for you.

It was, in a sense. But it is also a very honest document, and a small amount of vocabulary lets you read most of it. This guide is for engineers who write SQL daily and have been nodding politely at query plans.

## What a plan actually is

When you send a query, PostgreSQL does not run it as written. SQL says what you want. The planner decides how to get it: which indexes to use, in what order to join tables, and which join method to apply. The plan is that decision, shown as a tree.

Read it from the innermost, most indented lines outward. The deepest nodes run first and feed rows upward to their parents. The top line is the final result.

There are two commands to know. `EXPLAIN` shows the plan the planner would choose, with estimates, without running the query. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` actually runs the query and reports what really happened, including time and memory pages touched. Use the second for diagnosis. Be careful with it on statements that write data, because ANALYZE executes them. Wrap those in a transaction and roll back.

## A first plan, line by line

Take a simple lookup:

```
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM payments WHERE account_id = 4821;
```

A typical result looks like this:

```
Index Scan using payments_account_id_idx on payments
  (cost=0.43..52.10 rows=40 width=96)
  (actual time=0.031..0.210 rows=38 loops=1)
  Index Cond: (account_id = 4821)
  Buffers: shared hit=45
Planning Time: 0.120 ms
Execution Time: 0.260 ms
```

Break it down:

- **Index Scan using ...** is the method. The planner found an index on `account_id` and used it.
- **cost=0.43..52.10** is the planner's own unit of effort, not milliseconds. The first number is the cost to return the first row, the second to return all rows. Compare costs within one plan, never across machines.
- **rows=40** is the estimate. **actual rows=38** is the truth. These are close, which is good.
- **loops=1** says this node ran once. This number matters more than it looks, as we will see.
- **Buffers: shared hit=45** means 45 pages were found in memory. A `read` figure would mean pages fetched from disk.

That is a healthy plan. Short, estimated well, and cheap.

### Scan types you will meet

You will see the same handful of node types again and again.

**Seq Scan** reads the whole table. It is not automatically bad. For a small table, or a query that needs most rows, it is the fastest option. It is bad when it reads millions of rows to return a few.

**Index Scan** walks an index and fetches matching rows from the table. **Index Only Scan** answers entirely from the index when all needed columns are in it, skipping the table, provided the visibility information is up to date.

**Bitmap Heap Scan** sits between the two. It collects matching row locations from one or more indexes, then reads the table pages in order. You often see it when a filter matches a moderate share of rows, or when two indexes are combined.

The question is never "is there a Seq Scan". It is "does the amount of work match the number of rows I actually need".

### Join methods

Joins have three main strategies, and each suits different shapes of data.

**Nested Loop** takes each row from the outer side and looks up matches on the inner side. It is excellent when the outer side is small and the inner side has an index. It is a disaster when the outer side is large and the inner lookup is slow, because the cost multiplies.

**Hash Join** builds an in memory hash table from one input and probes it with the other. It handles large, unsorted inputs well. If the hash table does not fit in `work_mem`, it spills to disk, and you will see batches greater than one.

**Merge Join** walks two sorted inputs together. It shines when both sides are already sorted, perhaps by index, and is common on big joins.

None is best. The planner picks based on estimated row counts, which brings us to the most important habit.

## Compare estimates to actuals

Most slow plans have one cause: the planner guessed wrongly about how many rows it would see. It then picked a strategy that is right for the guess and wrong for reality.

Scan down the plan and compare `rows=` with the `actual rows=` for each node. A gap of a few percent is normal. A gap of ten times or a thousand times is the bug.

```
Nested Loop
  (cost=0.43..120.00 rows=5 width=64)
  (actual time=0.05..9800.00 rows=250000 loops=1)
```

Here the planner expected five rows and got a quarter of a million. It chose a nested loop for a few rows, then ground through a lot of them. The fix is not in the join, it is in the estimate.

Common reasons for bad estimates:

- Statistics are stale. Run `ANALYZE` on the table, or check that autovacuum is keeping up.
- Columns are correlated. The planner assumes `city` and `postcode` are independent, but they are not. Extended statistics with `CREATE STATISTICS` can describe the dependency.
- A function or expression hides the column from statistics. A filter on `lower(email)` has no stats unless there is an expression index.
- The value is skewed. One tenant owns most rows, and the default sample does not capture it well. Raising the statistics target for that column can help.

### The loops trap

The `actual time` on a node is the average per loop, not the total. A node showing `actual time=0.5..0.6` with `loops=40000` has really taken about twenty seconds in total. Multiply before you conclude.

This catches people constantly in nested loops. An inner index scan that looks instant becomes the whole cost because it ran forty thousand times. Look for large `loops` values on the inner side of a nested loop, and ask whether a hash join would suit better, or whether the outer side returned far more rows than expected.

## Sorts, memory and disk

Look for `Sort Method`. `quicksort Memory: 120kB` is fine. `external merge Disk: 340000kB` means the sort spilled to disk because it exceeded `work_mem`. Before raising that setting globally, remember it applies per operation per connection, so a large value multiplied by many sessions can exhaust memory. Consider raising it for the specific session or query instead, or adding an index that delivers rows already sorted.

Similarly, a `Rows Removed by Filter` figure far larger than the rows returned is a sign that the database read lots of data and threw most of it away. An index on the filtered column, or a better composite index, usually helps.

## Indexes that actually help

A few rules of thumb hold up well.

For a query that filters on equality and sorts or ranges on another column, put the equality column first in a composite index. For frequently filtered subsets, a partial index such as one covering only `status = 'pending'` can be much smaller and faster. For columns you only read, an `INCLUDE` clause can enable index only scans.

And be sceptical of adding indexes by reflex. Every index slows writes and takes space. Add one after reading a plan that proves it would change the access path, then confirm with a new plan.

## A routine that works

When a query is slow, follow the same path every time. Run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on realistic data, not an empty development database. Find the node with the largest actual time, remembering to multiply by loops. Compare estimated and actual rows around it. Decide whether the cause is statistics, a missing index, or the shape of the query. Change one thing, then run the plan again.

Plans stop being frightening once you notice they are just a list of steps with a guess and a result beside each. Keep a few past plans from your own system and read them when nothing is wrong. The day something is, you will already know what normal looks like.

title: Why We Write the Runbook Before the Code
excerpt: Writing the page an exhausted engineer will need at night, before building the feature, exposes missing alerts, unsafe reruns and absent kill switches while they are still cheap to fix.
author: Altisly Studio
content:
## The 2 a.m. test

Every system eventually has a bad night. A queue backs up, a provider times out, a migration half applies. The person who gets the alert is rarely the person who wrote the code, and they are rarely fully awake.

Our test for a feature is simple: could a tired engineer who has never seen this service fix it using only the page in front of them? We used to check that after launch. Now we check it before we write the first line.

## What the runbook forces

Writing the runbook first sounds like ceremony. In practice it is a design tool, because the document cannot be written until you can answer some uncomfortable questions.

- What does "broken" look like, and what will the alert actually say?
- Which dashboard shows the problem, and what is the first thing to look at?
- What is safe to restart, and what is not?
- How do you stop the damage before you understand the cause?
- Who do you wake up if the first three steps fail?

If you cannot answer these, the feature is not ready to build. You have found a missing metric, a missing kill switch or an operation that cannot be undone, and you found it while it is still cheap to fix.

## A short example

Suppose we are adding a nightly job that settles card payments into customer accounts. The draft runbook has a section titled "Settlement did not finish". Writing it, we realise there is no way to see which batch is stuck, so we add a batch status table. We realise rerunning the job could pay people twice, so we make settlement idempotent by batch ID. We realise the on call person needs a way to pause it, so we add a flag.

None of that was in the original ticket. All of it came from asking what someone would do at night.

## Keep it small and honest

A runbook is not a design document. Ours are a page or two: symptoms, first checks, safe actions, unsafe actions, escalation. We write commands the reader can paste, and we state plainly what we do not know yet.

The test of a runbook is whether it is specific. "Check the logs" is not a step. "Open the settlement dashboard, look at the batch status panel, and find any batch older than thirty minutes" is. Where a step needs judgement, we say what the judgement depends on, so the reader is not left guessing what the author had in mind.

We also treat it as code. It lives in the repository, changes with a pull request, and gets reviewed by someone who did not write the feature. After every real incident, the first follow up is a runbook edit.

## Where it does not fit

For a throwaway prototype, this is overkill. If nobody depends on the thing, skip it. The rule applies once a system carries money, records or anyone's working day.

## Try it once

Pick your next small feature. Before opening the editor, write the "it is broken at night" page. If it takes ten minutes, you were ready. If it takes an afternoon, you just saved yourself an incident.

title: Six Platforms, Small Team
excerpt: AI leverage in a studio does not show up as typing faster. It shows up as holding architectural context across a build large enough that a small team would previously have lost the thread.
author: Altisly Studio
content:
## The question we set out to answer

Altisly started as an experiment with a narrow question attached: how much serious software can a small, AI equipped studio actually ship?

Six platforms later, across treasury, payments, identity and healthcare, we have an answer that is more specific than the one we expected.

## Where the leverage is not

It is not in typing. Code generation speeds up the part of the job that was never the bottleneck. A team that could not previously agree on a data model does not ship faster because the boilerplate arrives quicker. It ships a larger amount of the wrong thing.

It is not in the first eighty percent of a feature either. That part was always tractable. The last ten percent, the part where an operation can actually depend on the software, is the part that decides whether the build was worth doing, and it is stubbornly resistant to speed.

## Where it actually is

The leverage is in holding context.

A build with five frontend applications, two services and a shared framework has a coherence problem long before it has a capacity problem. The naming drifts. The error envelope is one shape here and another shape there. A convention agreed in March is quietly abandoned in June because nobody was holding it.

A small team with AI leverage can keep that thread. Conventions get applied consistently because they can be restated, checked and enforced across a codebase larger than one person can hold. Architectural decisions stay written down, because writing them down stopped being expensive. The framework underneath stays coherent because drift gets caught while it is still cheap.

That is what let a small team carry six platforms without any of them turning into the one nobody wants to open.

## What has to be true first

This only compounds on top of things that were already made explicit.

You need decisions written down, with what was rejected and why. You need conventions stated rather than absorbed. You need contracts generated from a single source rather than maintained in two places by agreement.

A studio that has none of those gets a faster version of its existing incoherence.

## What this means commercially

The traditional split had strategy on one side, producing a document, and execution on the other, producing software, with a translation loss in the middle that nobody owned.

A small team that can architect and build removes the translation. When we advise on a compliance bottleneck, the deliverable is the engine that encodes the rule, not the manual describing it. When we work with a founder, we hold the ledger design rather than reviewing somebody else's.

That is only viable at a small size if the team can carry more system per person than it used to. Which is exactly the thing this experiment was testing.

## Where we are now

Still compounding. The domains look scattered from outside, and they are not: every one of them is operations heavy, and in every one the workflow is the product.

The honest caveat is that leverage magnifies whatever architecture it is pointed at. Point it at a system whose boundaries were never decided and it will help you build the mess faster, and larger, and with better test coverage.

title: Digital Public Infrastructure: Lessons From India's Stack
excerpt: India's identity, payments and consent layers are best understood as shared protocols, not apps. We look at what the design teaches, what does not transfer, and what builders should take from it.
author: Altisly Strategy Team
content:
## A design idea, not a product

When people talk about India's digital stack, they often describe it as a set of apps. It is closer to a set of agreements. Identity through Aadhaar, payments through UPI, and consent based data sharing through the Account Aggregator framework are protocols and rules that many private and public parties build on. The government supplies the rails. Banks, fintechs and developers supply the products.

That distinction is the most useful thing to take from the Indian experience, and it travels better than any single technology. This piece looks at what the design teaches, where it is specific to India, and what a country such as Nigeria or Ghana might reasonably borrow. It is a discussion of design, not a verdict on any government or its choices.

## The pattern: thin public layer, thick private layer

The stack works because the public layer is deliberately small. UPI is an interoperable payment system run under the National Payments Corporation of India. It defines how money moves between participating banks and apps and leaves the customer experience to others. A user can pay from one provider's app to an account at a different bank, and neither side needs a bilateral deal.

The same shape appears elsewhere in the stack. A shared identity layer lets providers verify a person without each building their own onboarding. A consent layer lets a person choose to share financial data with a lender for a stated purpose. In each case the public component answers one narrow question reliably and then gets out of the way.

Compare this with a platform model, where one organisation owns the whole experience. Platforms can move fast, but they concentrate power and become a single point of commercial and technical failure. A protocol model moves slower to set up and then lets competition happen on top.

## Three lessons that hold up

**Interoperability is the product.** Payments are worth little if they only work inside one network. The design goal was that any participant could connect to any other through a common standard, with open specifications and published rules. When you evaluate a national initiative, ask first who can plug in, on what terms, and who decides.

**Make the right thing cheap.** Low or zero cost for basic person to person transfers was a policy decision as much as a technical one. It pushed adoption by making the new rail the easy default. Whether a rail is free, subsidised or priced is a question every country answers differently, but the principle stands: if the rail costs more than the alternative, people will not move.

**Consent must be real.** The data sharing layer is built on the idea that a person, not an institution, decides who sees their records. That is a design constraint, with consent artefacts, purpose limits and revocation. It echoes the logic of modern data protection laws such as GDPR and the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, which also centre lawful purpose and individual control.

## What does not transfer cleanly

Honest analysis has to include the limits.

India's context is specific. A very large single market, a national identity programme with broad enrolment, a central bank with a clear mandate and a long political commitment to the approach all shaped the outcome. Smaller or more fragmented markets will not replicate the scale effects, and some of the cost advantages depend on volume.

The identity layer has also drawn serious debate there, about privacy, exclusion when authentication fails, and whether participation was effectively required. Those arguments are part of the lesson. A shared identity system is powerful precisely because it is hard to opt out of, and that power needs oversight, legal limits and a way to challenge errors. Nigeria and Ghana, each with their own national identity programmes and instant payment systems, face versions of the same trade offs.

And infrastructure does not remove the need for institutions. Dispute handling, fraud response, grievance processes and clear liability rules are what let ordinary people trust the rails. The technology is the visible part. The rulebook is the load bearing part.

## What builders should take from it

If you build products on top of public infrastructure, a few habits help.

- Design for the protocol, not for one provider's interpretation of it. Keep your integration layer thin so a change in the rules does not become a rewrite.
- Treat the shared rail as unreliable at the edges. Timeouts, duplicate callbacks and delayed settlement are normal, so build reconciliation in from the start.
- Store consent and purpose with the data. If you cannot say why you hold a record and who agreed to it, you cannot defend it.
- Expect the rules to change. Public infrastructure evolves under policy pressure, and the teams that survive are the ones whose architecture assumed it.

## Questions worth asking of any national stack

When a government or regulator announces a digital public infrastructure plan, a short checklist keeps the conversation grounded:

- Is the specification open, so independent parties can implement it?
- Who governs changes, and how are participants consulted?
- What happens when a person is wrongly rejected or wrongly charged?
- Can a private provider build a competitive product on top without special access?

The strongest part of the Indian approach is not any one system. It is the habit of building small, shared, rule based layers and leaving the rest to the market. That habit is available to every country, whatever its size.

title: What a Good Audit Log Actually Records
excerpt: A finance lead asks who approved a payment, and the log says only that something was updated. Here is what an audit trail needs to record so it answers real questions under pressure.
author: Altisly Engineering
content:
Picture a finance lead who opens a ticket on Monday morning: a supplier payment went out on Friday, nobody remembers approving it, and the amount looks wrong. Engineering opens the audit log. It says `payment.updated`, a timestamp, and a user ID. That is all. The log exists, it is full of rows, and it cannot answer a single question anyone is asking.

Most audit logs fail this way. They were built to satisfy a checkbox, so they record that something happened rather than what, by whom, and why it was allowed.

## Start with the questions, not the events

An audit log is read under pressure, usually by someone who is not an engineer, usually after something has gone wrong. So design it backwards from the questions that person will ask:

- Who did this, and were they acting as themselves or on behalf of someone else?
- What exactly changed, from what value to what value?
- When did it happen, and in what order relative to other changes?
- Where did the request come from?
- Which rule or permission allowed it?
- Was it a person, a scheduled job, or an integration?

If an entry cannot answer all six, it will eventually fail you. Write these questions on the wall before you design the schema. They make most arguments about what to log short.

## The shape of a useful entry

A good entry is a small, boring, consistent record. Here is roughly what we would expect to see:

```
{
  "id": "01J...",
  "occurredAt": "2026-05-22T14:03:11.482Z",
  "actor": { "type": "user", "id": "u_4821", "onBehalfOf": null },
  "action": "payment.approve",
  "target": { "type": "payment", "id": "pay_9910" },
  "before": { "status": "pending", "amount": 450000 },
  "after": { "status": "approved", "amount": 450000 },
  "context": { "ip": "203.0.113.7", "session": "s_77a", "requestId": "r_c31" },
  "authorisation": { "role": "finance_approver", "policy": "dual_approval" }
}
```

A few choices in there are deliberate.

The **actor** has a type. Users, service accounts and scheduled jobs behave differently, and "who" is meaningless if you cannot tell a human from a cron job. The `onBehalfOf` field matters for support impersonation and delegated approvals, where the person clicking is not the person accountable.

The **action** is a verb in a stable vocabulary, not a free text string. `payment.approve` can be counted, filtered and alerted on. "User approved a payment, I think" cannot.

The **before and after** values are the part teams skip because they are awkward. They are also the part that settles disputes. Storing only the new value tells you what the record is now, which you can already see. The diff is the evidence.

The **authorisation** field records why the action was allowed at the moment it happened. Roles change. If someone loses their approver role next month, you still need to know they held it on Friday.

## What not to record

More is not better. Two categories of data do damage when they land in an audit log.

First, secrets. Passwords, tokens, full card numbers and raw identity documents do not belong in a log that many people can read and that you are required to keep for years. Record that a credential was changed, never the credential. For personal data, store references and hashes where you can, and be deliberate about anything that would make the log itself a data protection liability. Under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 and under GDPR, a log full of personal data is still personal data.

Second, noise. Logging every read, every page view and every health check buries the entries that matter. Reads of sensitive records are worth logging, such as someone opening a customer's full file. Reads of a dashboard are not. Decide by asking whether a regulator, an auditor or an angry customer could plausibly ask who looked at this.

## Make it hard to change

An audit log that administrators can edit is a diary. The value of the record comes from the fact that nobody, including the people who run the system, can quietly rewrite it.

There are a few practical levels of protection, and you do not need all of them on day one:

- Application code can only insert, never update or delete. Enforce this with database permissions, not good intentions.
- Each entry includes a hash of the previous one, so a gap or an edit breaks the chain and is detectable.
- Logs are copied to a separate store with different credentials, so compromising the application database does not let someone clean up behind themselves.

## Write the entry in the same transaction

The most common technical flaw we see is logging after the fact. The business change commits, then the application tries to write the audit entry, and the second step fails or the process dies between them. You now have a change with no record.

Write the audit entry in the same database transaction as the change itself. Either both exist or neither does. If the log lives in a different system, use an outbox table inside the transaction and ship from there. It adds a little plumbing and removes an entire class of "we lost the evidence" incidents.

### Retention, access and the audit of the audit

Decide how long you keep entries before someone asks. Financial records often carry multi year retention expectations, and sector regulators set their own. Check the rules that apply to you rather than guessing, and write the period down.

Decide who can read the log. Access to an audit trail is itself sensitive, and reading it should be logged too. It sounds circular. It is not: the first time someone investigates a colleague, you will want proof that the investigation was itself authorised.

Finally, test the log the way you would test a backup. Once a quarter, pick a real event and try to reconstruct it from the log alone, without asking an engineer. If a finance lead can answer the Monday morning questions from the screen, the log works. If they need a developer and a database console, it does not yet.

## A small place to begin

If your current log is a thin list of event names, you do not need a rebuild. Add actor type, before and after values and the request ID to your most sensitive action, probably payments or permission changes. Write it in the same transaction. Ship that one action well, and use it as the template for the rest.

title: Energy Is the Hidden Constraint on Tech in Emerging Markets
excerpt: Unreliable power shapes budgets, product design and hosting choices long before it shows up in a pitch. How builders can design for interruption and treat energy as a real cost.
author: Altisly Studio
content:
## The cost nobody puts in the pitch deck

Ask a founder what limits their growth and you will hear about talent, funding or customers. Ask an operations lead in Lagos what actually interrupted last week and the answer may be simpler: the power went off. Electricity is the quiet constraint underneath nearly every other plan.

This is not a complaint about any one country. It is an observation about how reliable power shapes technology businesses, and what builders can do when it is not guaranteed.

## Where the constraint shows up

Software feels weightless, but it runs on machines that need power, in buildings that need cooling, connected by networks that need power too. When supply is unreliable, the effects spread in every direction.

Offices and studios run generators or inverters, and fuel or battery capacity becomes a line in the budget. Servers kept on premises need uninterruptible supplies. Mobile towers and network equipment depend on backup power, so connectivity can degrade when the grid fails. Staff working from home lose work hours to outages that are nobody's fault.

For a business, this means a cost that is both direct and variable. Diesel, solar installations, batteries and maintenance are real expenses. So is the lost productivity when none of them is enough. A company in a region with stable power does not carry these costs, which is one reason comparing operating budgets across markets can mislead.

## What it does to product design

The more interesting effect is on what we build and how.

If a clinic's power fails during the day, its software should not lose a half completed patient record. If a point of sale terminal loses connection, the shop should still be able to sell. If a field agent's phone battery is low, the app should not demand a long sync before it will work.

This pushes designers toward several habits.

- **Offline first behaviour.** Let the application work without a connection, save locally, and reconcile when the network returns.
- **Saving progressively.** Never hold a long form hostage to a single submit.
- **Light data use.** Smaller payloads and efficient sync reduce both data cost and battery drain.
- **Graceful recovery.** Assume interruptions will happen mid operation and make resuming safe, so duplicate and partial actions are handled rather than hoped away.

Software built in markets with stable power often assumes none of this. The result is products that work well in a demo and badly in the field. Building for interruption tends to produce software that is better everywhere, since networks fail even in places with excellent grids.

## Infrastructure decisions get harder

Hosting is another place where energy is part of the decision. Running serious computing capacity locally means securing power, cooling and connectivity at a scale few small companies can manage. Many therefore rely on cloud regions elsewhere, which brings latency and, where rules require it, data residency questions.

Meanwhile, the growth of compute heavy workloads, including machine learning, makes electricity use a more visible cost for everyone. Where power is expensive or scarce, efficiency stops being a nicety. Choosing a smaller model, caching results and avoiding wasteful processing are economic decisions as much as technical ones.

## Practical responses

For a team operating where power is uncertain, a few measures pay back reliably.

Make an honest inventory of what must stay up. Not everything needs the same protection. Payment processing, patient records and communication tools justify backup power and redundancy. A staff intranet may not.

Test your failure modes on purpose. Turn off the network, kill the process mid write, run the app on a nearly flat phone. You will learn more in an hour than in a month of reading logs.

Treat energy as a recurring line in the budget, not a surprise. If a solar and battery system pays for itself over time, model it like any other investment. Where it does not, plan the generator fuel.

And design transactions to be repeatable. Idempotent operations, durable queues and clear status states mean an interruption becomes a delay rather than a loss.

## The opportunity inside the constraint

There is a more optimistic reading. Businesses that learn to operate through unreliable infrastructure develop skills that others lack: resilient design, efficient use of resources, careful thought about failure. Products built under these conditions can travel well, because they were never allowed to assume everything works.

None of this makes the constraint pleasant or fair. Reliable power is a public good, and no amount of clever engineering replaces it. But while the problem remains, builders have a choice between pretending it is not there and designing around it. The second approach produces better software and more honest budgets.

## One question to ask this week

Look at your product and ask what happens in the middle of an outage. Not the beginning, not the end, the middle. If you do not know, find out before your customers do.

title: Open Weights or Hosted APIs: A Practical Comparison
excerpt: Hosted APIs are fast to start and open weights give control, but the real costs sit elsewhere. A practical way to choose, test and keep your options open.
author: Altisly Strategy Team
content:
## A decision that looks like a technical one

A team wants to add a language model to a product. Someone asks whether to call a hosted API or run an open weights model on their own servers. It sounds like an infrastructure question. It is really a question about cost, control, risk and who you want to depend on.

There is no universal answer, and anyone who offers one is selling something. What follows is a way to think it through, based on the trade offs rather than on any specific model, since specific models change every few months and this advice should outlast them.

## Two terms, used carefully

**Hosted APIs** mean you send requests to a provider's servers and receive responses. The provider runs the model, the hardware and the scaling. You pay per use, typically by the amount of text processed.

**Open weights** means the trained model's parameters are published so you can download and run them yourself. This is not always the same as open source. Licences vary, and some restrict commercial use or impose conditions, so read the terms for the specific model you intend to use. Running the model is then your job, on your own hardware or rented machines.

There is also a middle path: managed services that host open weights models for you. That gives you some of the portability of open weights with less operational burden, at the price of some of the control.

## What hosted APIs do well

Speed to a working product is the main advantage. You can have something running in an afternoon. There is no hardware to buy, no serving software to tune, and no capacity planning. Providers also tend to offer their most capable models through their APIs first, and those models are often hard to match with anything you can run yourself.

Costs scale with usage, which suits experiments and uneven demand. If you have ten users, you pay for ten users. You also inherit the provider's investment in reliability, safety measures and ongoing improvement.

The weaknesses are the mirror image. You depend on a third party for availability, pricing and terms. Models are updated or retired on the provider's schedule, which can change your product's behaviour. Your data leaves your environment, which raises questions that depend on the provider's terms and on your obligations.

## What open weights do well

Control is the central advantage. You decide where the model runs, which version you use and when, if ever, it changes. Behaviour stays stable because nothing updates beneath you. You can run it inside your own network, which can simplify some data protection and residency questions, since personal data need not be sent to an external provider.

You can also adapt the model. Fine tuning on your own material, constraining outputs and tuning for a narrow task are all open to you, within the model's licence. For a well defined, high volume task, a smaller model that you run yourself can be both cheaper and fast enough.

The cost is operational. You need people who can deploy, monitor and scale model serving. You pay for hardware whether or not it is busy. Capable GPUs can be expensive or hard to obtain, and power and cooling matter, especially where electricity is unreliable. Quality may lag behind the strongest hosted models for demanding reasoning tasks, though the gap varies and shifts over time.

## Where the money really goes

Comparing the two on cost is trickier than it looks.

- **Hosted APIs** have a variable cost with almost no fixed cost. The bill grows with traffic and with the length of prompts and outputs.
- **Self hosting** has a largely fixed cost: hardware or rented capacity, plus the engineering time to keep it running. The cost per request falls as utilisation rises.

So the crossover depends on volume and on how steady it is. At low or spiky volume, hosted is usually cheaper once you count staff time honestly. At high, steady volume, self hosting can win, provided you keep the hardware busy. Many teams underestimate the people cost, and overestimate their utilisation.

## Questions that settle most cases

Rather than debate in the abstract, answer these for your specific use.

- **What data goes in?** If it is sensitive or regulated, can you accept a provider's terms, or must it stay within your environment? Check the data protection rules that apply to you.
- **How hard is the task?** Classification, extraction and routing often work well on smaller models. Open ended reasoning or complex writing may need the strongest available.
- **How stable must behaviour be?** If your product breaks when outputs shift slightly, pinning a version you control has real value.
- **What is your volume?** Estimate it honestly, including peaks.
- **Who will run it?** Do you have, or want to hire, the skills to operate model serving?
- **What if the provider changes?** Prices, limits and terms can move. How exposed are you?

## Risks people forget

With hosted APIs, the forgotten risk is concentration. If one provider sits under several of your features, a pricing change, an outage or a policy shift hits all of them together. Rate limits can also bite at exactly the moment your product succeeds. Read the terms on how your inputs may be stored or used, and whether you can opt out of any retention.

With open weights, the forgotten risk is staleness and security. A model you run does not improve unless you upgrade it, and the serving software around it needs patching like any other service. Safety behaviour, such as refusing harmful requests or resisting manipulation, is also partly your responsibility rather than the provider's. Budget for testing it.

In both cases, a model's outputs can be wrong in fluent, convincing ways. Neither choice removes the need for human review where mistakes are costly.

## You can mix them

The choice is not permanent, and it is rarely all or nothing. A sensible pattern is to start with a hosted API to prove the use case and learn what the task really requires. Keep the model behind a thin interface in your own code, so swapping it is a configuration change rather than a rewrite. Build an evaluation set from real examples, so you can test alternatives on your own task rather than on a public leaderboard.

Later, move the high volume, well understood parts to a model you run, and keep the hosted API for the hard or rare cases. Route requests to the cheapest option that does the job well enough.

## Evaluate on your own work

Public benchmarks tell you how a model performs on someone else's questions. Collect a few dozen to a few hundred real examples from your own workflow, with the answers a careful person would give. Run each candidate against them and read the failures yourself. A cheaper model that gets your task right most of the time may beat a famous one, and you will only know by testing.

## A closing rule of thumb

Start hosted, measure honestly, and move to open weights only when volume, data constraints or the need for control give you a clear reason. Whichever you choose, keep your own evaluation and your own abstraction layer. They are the assets that stay yours, and they are what let you change your mind without paying for it twice.

title: Why System > Person is the Only Way to Scale
excerpt: Key-man risk is the silent killer of growing enterprises. Here is how we engineer systems that institutionalize knowledge and ensure zero operational disruption.
author: Altisly Engineering
content:
## The Problem with Hero Culture

In early-stage companies, 'hero culture' is celebrated. When the database goes down at 2 AM, the lead engineer stays up until dawn fixing it. When a massive reconciliation error happens, the Head of Finance spends their weekend manually tracing missing funds in Excel.

But as organizations scale, relying on heroes becomes an existential risk. What happens when your Treasury ALM Lead takes leave? What happens when your principal architect moves on? If the system breaks down because a specific person isn't in the room, you don't have a business—you have a dependency.

## Institutionalizing Knowledge into Code

At Altisly, our core philosophy is **System > Person**. We believe that every operational workflow, every manual reconciliation step, and every complex compliance rule should be institutionalized into code.

Take treasury operations as an example. We frequently see companies relying on a single individual to manage Asset Liability Management (ALM) and publish liquidity reports across multiple banking partners. The risk here is immense: a single failure could lead to a liquidity crunch.

To solve this, we build Treasury Systems that automate Cash Positioning. We wire up direct API integrations with banking partners, pipe the data into a unified ledger, and automate the daily 09:00 Kaizen reporting. The system becomes the source of truth, not the person.

## Designing for Resilience

Transitioning to a System > Person model requires three architectural shifts:

1. **Deterministic Data Flows:** Eliminate spreadsheets. If data needs to move from a payment gateway to an ERP, it must happen via an automated ETL pipeline that logs every failure and retries automatically.
2. **Automated Compliance:** Compliance should not rely on manual reviews. We architect AML and KYC engines that flag anomalies deterministically based on machine-readable rules.
3. **Immutable Ledgers:** The core of any financial or enterprise system must be an immutable, double-entry ledger. When an error occurs, you shouldn't need a forensic accountant to find it—the ledger should provide a perfect cryptographic audit trail.

When you build systems this way, you don't just reduce risk. You free up your smartest people to focus on strategy and growth, rather than maintenance and firefighting.

title: Migrations That Can Run Twice
excerpt: A migration that dies halfway should be a rerun, not a lost weekend. How to write schema changes that are safe to repeat, resume and test.
author: Altisly Engineering
content:
## The migration that failed at step forty

You start a database migration on a Friday afternoon. It runs for a while, then dies on the fortieth of eighty statements because of a lock timeout. Now the schema is half changed. Rerunning from the top fails because the first thirty nine statements already ran. Rerunning from step forty means reading the logs, guessing the state and typing by hand. The weekend is gone.

The fix is not better luck. It is writing migrations that can safely run twice.

## What idempotent means for schema changes

An idempotent migration reaches the same end state whether it runs once, twice or after a partial failure. It checks what already exists before it acts, and does nothing when the work is already done.

This is a different mindset from the usual one, where each migration is assumed to run exactly once, in order, against a known state. That assumption holds in a tidy development environment. It fails in production, where a runner can be interrupted, a connection can drop, a deployment can be retried by an impatient colleague, or two processes can start at once.

## Make each statement safe to repeat

Most databases give you the tools. In PostgreSQL, for instance, many statements accept guards:

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS invoices (
  id bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  total numeric NOT NULL
);

ALTER TABLE invoices
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS currency text;

CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_invoices_currency
  ON invoices (currency);
```

Running that block twice does no harm. Dropping things follows the same pattern with `IF EXISTS`.

Not every change has a built in guard. Adding a constraint, changing a column type or creating a trigger may need a check against the catalogue first, wrapped in a small procedural block that tests whether the change is already applied. It is more typing, but the typing is cheap compared with a recovery.

## Use transactions, within limits

Where the database supports transactional schema changes, wrap each migration in one transaction. If anything fails, everything rolls back and the schema returns to its prior state. PostgreSQL does this well for most statements. Some operations cannot run inside a transaction, such as creating an index concurrently, and these need separate handling.

Do not assume every database behaves the same way. Some commit schema changes implicitly, which means a failure midway leaves you partly migrated, and idempotency matters even more. Know what yours does before you rely on it.

## Track what has run

A migration runner keeps a table recording which migrations have been applied. That table is the source of truth, and it should be updated in the same transaction as the change wherever possible, so the record and the reality cannot drift.

Add a lock so that two runners cannot work at once. An advisory lock held for the duration of the run is a simple way to stop a second process from colliding with the first. If you run migrations across many separate schemas, as multi tenant systems sometimes do, track the version per schema, so a failure on one does not hide the state of the others.

## Separate the change from the data

Schema changes and data changes behave differently, and mixing them makes failure worse. Adding a column is quick. Back filling ten million rows is not.

Do the structural change first, as a small, fast and idempotent step. Then run the back fill as its own job, in batches, with a way to resume from where it stopped. A common safe pattern is to add the new column as nullable, back fill in the background, and only then add the constraint that requires it. Each stage can fail and be retried without damaging the others.

## Roll forward, not back

Teams spend a lot of effort on down migrations. In practice, many are never tested, and a rollback that deletes a column also deletes whatever was written to it since. For many production situations, the safer approach is to prefer rolling forward: write a new migration that fixes the problem.

That works best when changes are made in compatible steps. Add the new thing, deploy code that uses both, move traffic, and only later remove the old thing. At every point, either version of the application can run against the schema. This is sometimes called expand and contract, and it also happens to make each individual migration smaller and easier to repeat.

## Test the second run

The simplest test for idempotency is the most telling: run every migration twice against a fresh database and confirm the second run changes nothing. Add it to your continuous integration. Better still, test an interrupted run by killing the runner partway and starting it again.

Also rehearse against a copy of production data when you can. Problems that never appear on a small test database, such as lock waits and slow back fills, appear immediately on a large one.

## A habit worth keeping

Before merging a migration, ask one question: if this stopped halfway and someone ran it again, what would happen? If the answer is "I am not sure", the migration is not finished.
