The goal is not to make failure impossible. It is to make recovery boring, so that the Friday afternoon failure ends with a rerun and not a weekend.

title: Why Hospital Software Fails at the Front Desk
excerpt: Hospital software often fails in the first ten minutes of a patient's visit. Why front desk workflows break, and what good registration, search and billing look like in practice.
author: Altisly Studio
content:
## The first person a patient meets

Walk into almost any busy hospital and watch the front desk for ten minutes. Someone is answering a phone, someone is holding a folder, someone is explaining for the third time where the lab is, and a queue is forming behind a patient whose record cannot be found. This is where hospital software meets reality, and it is where a surprising amount of it fails.

The failure is rarely dramatic. The system does what its designers intended. It just does not match what the front desk actually has to do, so staff work around it, and the workarounds become the real process.

## Designed for the back office

A lot of hospital management software is built from the inside out. It starts with the database: patients, visits, charges, results. Screens are then added to expose each table, and the result is a system that is complete and exhausting to use.

The front desk has different needs. A receptionist handles many short interactions, each under time pressure, with a patient standing in front of them. They need to find a person fast, confirm who they are, check what is owed or booked, and send them to the right place. Every extra field, every required dropdown and every confirmation dialog is a few seconds multiplied across hundreds of patients a day.

When software optimises for completeness over speed, staff protect the queue by skipping fields, entering placeholder data or writing things on paper to be typed in later. The record is now worse than if the system had asked for less.

## Four ways it breaks

**Patient search that does not forgive.** Names are entered inconsistently. Spellings vary, middle names come and go, and phone numbers change. If search demands an exact match, staff create a new record rather than find the old one. Duplicates then spread through billing and clinical history, and cleaning them up is slow, careful work.

**Registration as an interrogation.** A new patient form that asks for thirty fields before the visit can start will be answered carelessly or not at all. Collect what is needed to begin care and bill sensibly, and let the rest be filled in over time.

**No view of the day.** Front desk staff need to see who is expected, who has arrived, who is with a clinician and who is waiting for results. If that picture requires opening four screens, they will keep it on a notepad.

**Unreliable when connectivity is not.** Power and network interruptions are ordinary in many facilities. A system that freezes or loses half a registration when the connection drops teaches staff to distrust it. Software that tolerates interruption, saves progressively and recovers gracefully earns patience it will otherwise lose.

## Billing starts at the front desk

Another quiet failure is the link between registration and money. Whether a patient pays directly, uses insurance or is covered by an employer, the front desk is where that is first established. If the system cannot capture the payer at registration, or cannot show what a visit is likely to cost, the problem surfaces later as disputed bills, delayed collection and awkward conversations at discharge.

Good hospital software treats payment status as part of the arrival, not a separate department's problem. It lets the front desk see the relevant information in the same place as the booking.

## What good looks like

The best front desk systems we can picture share a few traits.

- **Search that tolerates mess.** It matches partial names, phone numbers and approximate spellings, and shows enough to tell two similar people apart.
- **Short paths for common tasks.** Check in, book, collect payment and redirect should each take a few actions, not a tour of menus.
- **A single live view.** The state of the day is visible at a glance and updates without refreshing.
- **Forgiving data entry.** It accepts incomplete information when the situation demands, flags what is missing, and does not block the patient to do it.
- **Resilience.** It copes with a bad connection and does not lose work.

None of these is technically exotic. They are the result of watching how the work is really done.

## Build with the people at the desk

The most reliable way to avoid these failures is also the least glamorous: spend time at the front desk before writing the screen. Watch what staff do when the system is not helping. Note which fields they skip, which workarounds they have invented and what they keep on paper. Those are requirements the formal specification never captured.

Then put the receptionists in the room when the design is reviewed, not just the administrators and clinicians. Their view of the process is the most granular, and they are the ones who will either adopt the system or route around it.

## A modest test

Here is a test any hospital can run. Pick a typical morning and time how long it takes to register a returning patient who gives only a first name and a phone number. If it takes more than a minute, or if staff reach for a notebook, the software has not yet met the front desk. That is the place to start fixing it.

title: Architecting the Treasury of the Future
excerpt: How modern corporate treasuries are moving from spreadsheets to automated Cash Positioning.
author: Altisly Strategy Team
content:
## The Legacy Treasury Trap

Corporate treasury has historically been an exercise in looking backward. Treasury teams spend the first three hours of their day logging into a dozen different banking portals, downloading CSV files, and fighting with Excel macros just to figure out how much cash the company had yesterday.

This delay creates massive capital inefficiencies. When you don't have a Cash Positioning, you keep excess cash in low-yield accounts 'just in case,' or worse, you scramble to cover unexpected liquidity gaps.

## The Shift to Automated Cash Positioning

We are seeing a massive shift in how elite financial institutions manage their capital. The modern treasury is no longer an accounting function; it is a data engineering function.

By leveraging direct bank APIs and modern data warehousing (like Google BigQuery), we are building systems that automatically aggregate balances, monitor shifting deposit rates, and execute cross-corridor liquidity transfers without human intervention.

The goal is simple: 0% liquidity failure and 100% strategic focus.

title: Data Localisation and the Cost of Building Across Borders
excerpt: Keeping data inside a border sounds simple until it reaches your database, backups, vendors and budget. A look at what localisation costs and how to design for it.
author: Altisly Strategy Team
content:
## A rule that sounds simple

"Keep our citizens' data inside our borders." As a sentence, it is easy to agree with. As an engineering and business requirement, it touches your database, your backups, your logging, your support tooling, your vendors and your budget. The cost is rarely the storage itself. It is everything that was quietly assuming data could move freely.

This is an explainer on the trade offs. It is not legal advice, and the rules differ by country and sector, so always check the current requirements for the places you operate.

## What localisation actually means

The term covers a spectrum, and the differences matter.

At one end, **data residency** means a copy of the data must be stored in a particular country. At the other, **strict localisation** means the data must stay there, with limits or conditions on transfers abroad. In between, many laws allow transfers only if certain safeguards exist: an adequacy decision, contractual protections, or consent.

Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023, for example, sets conditions for transferring personal data out of the country rather than banning it outright. Other jurisdictions, and some sector regulators for banking, payments or health, can be stricter for particular categories of data. The practical lesson is to ask which data, under which rule, and for which regulator. "Localisation" is not one requirement.

## Why governments want it

The motives are worth taking seriously, whatever your view of the policies. Regulators want to be able to inspect records and enforce the law without depending on a foreign court. Governments want to protect citizens from data being exposed to weaker regimes. Some want to build domestic infrastructure and skills. And some are simply responding to genuine concerns about who can access sensitive information.

These are legitimate aims. The engineering question is how to meet them without breaking the product.

## Where the cost lands

Teams building across borders feel the cost in places they did not budget for.

- **Infrastructure.** A single global deployment becomes several regional ones. Each needs its own database, monitoring, deployment pipeline and on call attention.
- **Cloud availability.** Not every provider has a region in every country, and the services you rely on may not all be offered in the regions that do exist.
- **Data flows you forgot.** Analytics, error tracking, email providers, customer support tools and backups often copy personal data to servers elsewhere. Each is a transfer that needs accounting for.
- **Engineering complexity.** Features that join data across regions, such as global search or a worldwide dashboard, get harder or impossible.
- **Compliance overhead.** Someone must track which rules apply where, document the data flows and respond to audits.

The most expensive item is often the last one, because it never ends. Rules change, and your systems have to be able to follow.

## Design choices that make it cheaper

You cannot make the cost vanish, but you can decide where it falls.

**Separate the data from the product.** If personal data lives in a defined set of stores, and the rest of the application handles references or pseudonymous identifiers, you can localise the sensitive part without duplicating everything.

**Build region awareness in early.** Retrofitting the idea that a customer belongs to a region is painful. If each tenant or account carries a home region from the start, routing, storage and access can follow it.

**Map your data flows.** Keep a living record of where personal data goes, including third party tools. You cannot defend a transfer you do not know about.

**Choose vendors with eyes open.** Ask where a provider stores and processes data, who can access it, and whether you can choose the region. Make that part of procurement, not an afterthought.

**Minimise.** Data you never collect needs no residency plan. It is the cheapest control available.

## The trade off nobody can avoid

Localisation reduces some risks and creates others. Keeping data in one country may help regulators and reassure customers, but it can reduce redundancy, limit your choice of providers and make resilience harder. A small region may have fewer data centres, so a failure has fewer places to fail over to.

It also changes who can build. A large company can run several regional stacks. A small team cannot, and may decide to avoid a market altogether. That is a real cost to competition, and it is worth a policymaker's attention, even if the original objective is sound.

## A practical stance

If you are building for several countries, treat data location as a first class design input, like currency or language. Start by classifying your data, then map the rules to each class, then place systems accordingly.

Expect to revisit it. The aim is not to find a final answer, but to build systems whose location can be changed without rewriting the product. That flexibility is worth more than any single clever arrangement, because the rules will keep moving and your business will move with them.

title: Idempotency Keys Are a Product Feature
excerpt: A frozen screen and a second tap should never mean a double charge. Why idempotency keys belong in your product design, your documentation and your support tooling, not just your headers.
author: Altisly Engineering
content:
## The double charge nobody meant to cause

A customer taps pay. The screen freezes. The mobile network drops for a second, so they tap again. Somewhere behind the scenes, two requests arrive. If your system treats them as two separate payments, you have just taken money twice and created a support ticket, a refund and a person who is slightly less likely to trust you.

Most engineers know the cure: idempotency keys. Fewer treat them as something the customer, the integrator and the support team will actually experience. We think they deserve to be designed as a feature, not bolted on as a header.

## What an idempotency key actually promises

An idempotent operation produces the same result however many times you perform it. An idempotency key is how a caller tells your system, "this request is the same intended action as one I sent before."

The contract is simple to state. The client generates a unique key for each distinct action and sends it with the request. The server records the key along with the outcome. If the same key arrives again, the server does not repeat the action. It returns the original outcome.

That promise is what makes retries safe. Without it, a client that gets a timeout faces an impossible choice: retry and risk a duplicate, or stop and risk a loss. With it, the answer is always to retry.

## The details that decide whether it works

The idea is easy. The implementation is where it goes wrong.

**Store the key before the work, not after.** If you perform the action and then record the key, a crash in between leaves you with a completed action and no record. Record the key first, mark it in progress, do the work, then mark it complete, ideally in the same database transaction as the action itself.

**Handle concurrent duplicates.** Two identical requests can arrive at the same moment. A unique constraint on the key means only one gets to proceed. The other should wait or receive a clear response saying the original is still being processed, not run a second time.

**Bind the key to the request.** If a client reuses a key with a different amount or recipient, that is a bug, or worse. Store a fingerprint of the original request and reject mismatches with a clear error. Silently returning the old result for a different request would be confusing, and silently executing the new one would defeat the purpose.

**Return the original response.** Replaying should return what the first call returned, including a failure if it failed in a final way. Callers should not be able to tell the difference between the first answer and a repeat, other than perhaps a header noting it was a replay.

**Decide how long keys live.** Keys cannot be kept forever, but they must outlast any realistic retry window. A day is a common starting point for payment APIs. Whatever you choose, document it, because a retry after expiry looks like a new request.

## Why this belongs in the product

Here is the point where idempotency stops being an internal concern.

Integrators read your documentation to learn how to make your API safe. If keys are optional, hidden or vaguely described, they will skip them, and their customers will pay the price. If you require a key on every money moving endpoint, you push the right behaviour onto everyone by default.

Your own interface matters too. A mobile app that generates a key when a user opens a payment screen, and reuses it for every tap on that screen, gets double tap protection for free. A key generated at the moment of each tap provides none. That is a product decision as much as a technical one.

And support teams feel it. When a customer reports a duplicate, the first question is whether it was one action or two. If every request carries a key, and the key appears in your logs and your operator tools, the answer takes seconds rather than an afternoon.

## Where keys come from

Who generates the key? Almost always the client, since only the client knows whether two requests represent the same intent. A random identifier is usually enough. For some workflows, deriving the key from the business event is better: an invoice number combined with a payment attempt, say. That way two different systems that both try to pay the same invoice collide instead of both succeeding.

Avoid keys that reuse across unrelated actions, and avoid anything predictable that another party could guess and abuse.

## What keys do not do

Idempotency keys protect against duplicate submissions. They do not protect against a user who deliberately submits the same payment twice, and they should not. They also do not solve problems in downstream systems. If your provider does not honour keys, your retry may still create a duplicate on their side, so you need your own reconciliation to catch it.

## A short list for your next API

Before you ship a money moving endpoint, check the following:

- Is a key required rather than optional?
- Is it recorded before the action and committed with it?
- Are concurrent duplicates handled?
- Does a mismatched request with the same key fail loudly?
- Is the retention window documented?
- Can support find the key from a customer complaint?

An idempotency key is a small promise to a customer that pressing the button twice will not cost them twice. It is cheap to keep, and expensive to break.

title: Telemedicine After the Hype
excerpt: The urgency has faded and the grand claims with it. What remains is a set of tools that suit particular jobs, and a list of operational reasons why deployments stall.
author: Altisly Strategy Team
content:
## What the pandemic years taught us, and what they did not

For a while, telemedicine was presented as the thing that would remake healthcare. Then the urgency faded, patients went back to clinics, and some of the grand claims quietly went with them. What is left is less exciting and more useful: a set of tools that work well for specific jobs and badly for others.

This is a view from the operations and technology side. We are not offering clinical guidance, and nothing here is a statement about what treatment works. The question is simply what makes remote care function as a service, and why so many deployments stall.

## Where it genuinely fits

Remote consultations suit situations where the main thing needed is conversation, review or a decision, rather than a physical examination. Follow up appointments, medication reviews, test result discussions and routine check ins are common examples. Triage, where someone decides how urgently a person needs to be seen in person, is another.

The gains are practical. A patient avoids a long journey, a day off work and a waiting room. A clinic can see more people without more floor space. A specialist in one city can advise a generalist in another. None of that requires a dramatic claim about transforming medicine. It requires a reliable call and a sensible workflow.

## Where it does not

Plenty of care needs hands, instruments or a physical presence. Remote consultation cannot replace those, and it is irresponsible to pretend otherwise. Where it is used as a front door, a dependable route to in person care has to sit behind it. A telemedicine service that cannot hand a patient on to a real appointment is only a more convenient way of being stuck.

There is also a quieter problem. Remote care assumes the patient has a device, a decent connection, a private space and some comfort with the technology. In many places, including parts of Nigeria and Ghana, those assumptions fail often enough to matter. Data costs, power cuts and shared phones shape who can actually use the service. Designing for the patient who has a basic phone and a weak signal is not an edge case. It may be the main case.

## Why deployments stall

When telemedicine projects disappoint, the cause is rarely the video call. It is usually everything around it.

- **No link to the patient record.** If the clinician cannot see history during the consultation, and notes do not flow back into the record afterwards, the call becomes an isolated event and the work doubles.
- **Messy scheduling.** Remote and in person slots compete for the same clinicians. Without good scheduling, one starves the other or both overbook.
- **Unclear payment.** If nobody has decided how a remote consultation is billed, charged and reconciled, finance will treat it as an exception, and exceptions get ignored.
- **Weak follow through.** Prescriptions, referrals and lab requests that begin in a call need somewhere to go. If the patient has to repeat everything at the front desk, the benefit disappears.

Notice that none of these is a video problem. They are integration and process problems, which is why hospital management software matters more here than the conferencing tool does.

## Privacy and trust are part of the product

A consultation is a conversation about health. Where it happens, how it is recorded, and who can access the notes are not afterthoughts. In Nigeria, the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 treats health data as sensitive personal data, and similar duties apply under data protection laws in the UK and Ghana. That means clear consent, sensible access controls and a defensible position on what is stored and for how long.

Patients also judge a service by small signals: whether the clinician seems to know who they are, whether the call drops, whether they can reach someone afterwards. Trust is earned in those details.

## What a sensible approach looks like

If you run a clinic or a hospital group and you are considering remote services, start narrow. Pick one or two use cases where a physical examination is not the point, such as follow up reviews. Run them inside your existing patient record and scheduling system rather than beside it. Decide the billing rules before the first call, not after.

Plan the failure paths explicitly. What happens when the connection drops halfway? When a patient needs to be seen in person after all? When a prescription cannot be sent? A good service is measured less by the best call than by how it handles the bad one.

Finally, measure what matters operationally: how many consultations are completed, how often they end in an in person referral, how much staff time is saved or added. Be honest if the answer is that it adds work. That is useful information.

## A quieter kind of success

The most successful telemedicine we can imagine does not feel like a separate technology at all. It is one more way for a patient to reach a clinic, using the same record, the same schedule and the same billing as everything else. When it stops being a project and becomes a normal option, the hype has done its job and can be forgotten.

title: Open Banking in Nigeria and the UK Compared
excerpt: Both countries want customers to share their financial data safely, but they got there by different routes. A practical comparison of design, policy and what it means for builders.
author: Altisly Strategy Team
content:
## Two countries, one idea, different roads

Open banking sounds like a single thing. A customer lets a third party see their account data or start a payment, and the bank has to cooperate. In practice, the UK and Nigeria reached that idea by very different roads, and the differences explain a lot about what you can and cannot build in each place.

This is a comparison of design and policy, not a ranking. Both markets are still evolving, and details change, so treat what follows as a map of the main ideas rather than a legal reference.

## How the UK got there

The UK's version was largely a competition intervention. The competition regulator investigated retail banking and concluded that incumbent banks held too much power over customer data. The remedy was to require the largest banks to open their data to authorised third parties through standardised interfaces, with the customer's consent.

Two things followed from that origin. First, it was mandatory and specific. The biggest banks had to build to a common technical standard, delivered through a dedicated implementation body. Second, it was tied to a regulatory framework that already existed in Europe, the second Payment Services Directive, which created regulated roles for account information providers and payment initiation providers.

The result is a market with a well defined rulebook, a consent model that customers see in practice, and a certain amount of friction: re authentication requirements, consent renewals and the occasional uneven bank implementation.

## How Nigeria got there

Nigeria's path started from a different place. The central bank published open banking regulatory guidelines that set out how data should be shared between banks and other participants, including principles on consent, data classification and risk. The motivation was less about breaking up concentrated incumbents and more about widening access, supporting innovation and bringing more people into formal financial services.

The approach is also shaped by the existing infrastructure. Nigeria already has strong shared payment rails and a national identity layer in the form of the bank verification number. Open banking sits alongside those, and in practice there is a lot of attention on how it fits with them rather than replacing them.

Implementation has been phased and has depended on participants, standards and API availability maturing over time. If you are building, expect to confirm the current status of each institution's offering rather than assume uniform coverage.

## Where the designs differ

A few contrasts are worth holding in mind.

- **Origin.** The UK started from a competition remedy aimed at the largest banks. Nigeria started from a regulatory framework aimed at wider participation and access.
- **Standardisation.** The UK leans on a single, centrally defined API standard. Nigeria's framework sets principles and expectations, with the detail of implementation left to develop across participants.
- **Participants.** The UK rules lean heavily on defined, authorised roles. Nigeria's guidelines classify participants by risk and data type.
- **Surrounding infrastructure.** The UK sits inside a wider European style payments regime. Nigeria builds on local rails, identity systems and a fast growing digital payments habit.

None of these is simply better. A strict standard produces predictability. A looser framework can move quickly, but costs integrators more effort per bank.

## What this means if you are building

For a product team, the practical consequences are concrete.

In the UK, you will usually need to be authorised, or work under someone who is, before you touch regulated data or initiate payments. Your design problem is largely about consent: making renewal and revocation understandable, and handling the differences between banks gracefully.

In Nigeria, your design problem is often coverage and reliability. You may find that connecting to the institutions your customers actually use is the real work, and that you need fallbacks for the ones whose interfaces are not yet ready. Data protection obligations under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 also apply, so the consent and purpose limits you design around are not optional extras.

For a business operating in both, there is a trap: assuming that an integration pattern built for one market transfers cleanly. Consent flows, error behaviour, authentication steps and even the meaning of an account differ. It is better to build a thin internal abstraction and let each market sit behind its own adapter.

## The question of trust and security

Both systems depend on customers being willing to hand over access, and that willingness rests on trust. In practice that means strong authentication, clear explanation of what is being shared and for how long, and an easy way to withdraw consent. Designs that bury these steps get abandoned, or worse, produce customers who click through without understanding.

For providers, it also means thinking about liability. When something goes wrong in a chain that includes a bank, a third party and a customer, who is responsible? The answers are written down differently in each market, and a product team should read them before launch rather than after the first dispute.

## What each can learn from the other

The UK's experience shows that standards pay off, but that a standard alone does not guarantee a good customer experience. Consent fatigue and uneven bank behaviour were real lessons. Regulators and banks learned that user journeys have to be tested, not only specified.

Nigeria's setting offers a different lesson. Strong shared rails and identity infrastructure can give open banking a head start on things like verification and payments, if the new layer is designed to work with them instead of around them.

## A practical way to think about it

Do not copy the other market's playbook wholesale. Borrow the ideas that fit and test the rest.

If you are deciding where to build first, ask three questions. What data or payment function does my product actually need? Which institutions do my customers use, and are their interfaces ready today? And what consent and data protection obligations apply to the way I plan to use the data?

The honest answer in both countries is that the policy is only half the story. The other half is how well each bank has built, and how well you have designed for the days when something does not work.

title: The Rise of Tech-Enabled Consulting

title: Retries Without Regret: Backoff, Jitter and Budgets
excerpt: Retries feel free until they turn a small fault into an outage. How to use backoff, jitter and retry budgets so your service helps a struggling dependency instead of burying it.
author: Altisly Engineering
content:
Your payment service calls a provider. The provider times out. Your code tries again, and again, and within seconds every instance of your service is hammering a system that was already struggling. The retry that was meant to add resilience has become the outage.

This is one of the oldest failure patterns in distributed systems, and it keeps recurring because retries feel free. They are not. Each one is extra load, extra latency and, if you are careless, an extra side effect. Here is how we think about doing them properly.

## Decide what is worth retrying

Not every failure deserves another attempt. Retrying a request that failed because the input was invalid just produces the same failure more slowly.

Retry when the failure is likely to be transient:

- Network timeouts and connection resets.
- Server errors that signal temporary trouble, such as a 503 or a rate limit response.
- Lock conflicts and deadlock errors in your own database.

Do not retry validation errors, authentication failures, or anything that tells you the request itself is wrong. If a provider returns a client error, a second identical request will get a second identical answer.

The harder case is the timeout. A timeout does not tell you the request failed. It tells you that you stopped waiting. The operation may have completed on the other side. This is why retries and idempotency are inseparable: if the operation is not safe to repeat, you have no business repeating it automatically.

## Backoff: give the other side room

The simplest retry policy is to try again immediately. It is also the worst. If the dependency is overloaded, instant retries add pressure at exactly the wrong moment.

Exponential backoff fixes the first half of this. After the first failure, wait a short time. After the second, wait twice as long. After the third, twice again. The delay grows quickly enough that a struggling system gets breathing space.

```
delay = min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt)
```

The cap matters. Without it, the tenth retry might wait for minutes, and your user has long since given up. Pick a base delay that suits the call, perhaps a hundred milliseconds for an internal service, and a cap that matches how long the caller can sensibly wait.

## Jitter: stop everyone retrying together

Backoff alone has a flaw. If a hundred clients all fail at the same instant, they will all wait the same delay and all retry at the same instant. The load arrives in synchronised waves.

Jitter adds randomness to break the pattern. Instead of waiting exactly the computed delay, wait a random amount up to it:

```
delay = random_between(0, min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt))
```

This is often called full jitter, and it spreads retries across the window rather than stacking them at the edges. It looks slightly odd, since some retries will fire almost immediately, but the aggregate behaviour is far gentler on the dependency. There are variations, such as keeping a minimum delay and jittering only above it. The principle is the same: desynchronise your clients.

## Budgets: limit the total damage

Backoff and jitter govern the timing of one request. They say nothing about the volume of retries across the whole service. That is where a retry budget helps.

Imagine each service allows retries only up to a fixed fraction of its normal traffic, say a small percentage of requests in a recent window. When the dependency is healthy, almost nothing is retried and the budget is never touched. When it fails broadly, the budget runs out quickly, and the service stops adding retry load rather than multiplying it.

Without a budget, the maths turns against you. If every request is allowed three retries, a complete outage multiplies traffic to the dependency by four at the worst possible moment. And if the call passes through several layers, each retrying three times, the multiplication compounds. A budget turns "up to N attempts per request" into "at most this much extra load overall", which is the number you actually care about.

## Retry in one place only

A subtle trap is layered retries. Your HTTP client retries. Your SDK retries. Your service wrapper retries. Your job queue retries the whole job. A single failed call can fan into dozens of attempts, none of which any layer knows about.

Pick one layer to own retries for each call, usually the one closest to the business meaning of the operation, and disable the rest. Document it. When someone debugging an incident asks how many times a payment call is attempted, the answer should be one number, not a research project.

## Pair retries with timeouts and breakers

Retries need a deadline. Set an overall time limit for the operation, and make every attempt and every wait respect it. A request that has already taken too long to be useful should fail, not queue another try.

A circuit breaker complements this. After enough consecutive failures, it stops sending calls to the dependency for a short period and fails fast instead. That protects the dependency, and it protects your own threads and connections from piling up behind a dead service. Retries handle brief faults. Breakers handle sustained ones.

One more caution: honour what the dependency tells you. If a response carries a hint about when to come back, such as a Retry-After header on a rate limit, use that instead of your own schedule. The server knows more about its own recovery than your formula does. And never retry in a tight loop inside a request that a user is waiting on; fail quickly and let a background process pick the work up.

## Make retries observable

If you cannot see retries, you cannot tune them. Log or count each retry with the reason, the attempt number and the dependency involved. Watch the retry rate as a signal in its own right: a quiet climb in retries is often the first sign of a degrading provider, well before errors reach users.

## A short checklist

Before you ship a retry policy, check that:

- The operation is idempotent, or carries an idempotency key.
- Only transient errors are retried.
- Delays grow exponentially, are capped, and include jitter.
- A budget or breaker limits total retry volume.
- Exactly one layer is responsible for retrying.
- There is an overall deadline.

Think of a retry as spending someone else's capacity on your behalf, and ask whether you would spend it that freely if the bill came to you.

Retries are a loan against the future health of your system. Used sparingly and with limits, they hide small faults. Used carelessly, they turn small faults into large ones. The regret comes from having never set the terms.

title: A Plain English Guide to FX Spreads
excerpt: Your bank quoted a worse rate than the one you saw online, and nobody lied. Here is how spreads work, where businesses lose money on them, and how to measure what you really paid.
author: Altisly Strategy Team
content:
## The rate you were quoted is not the rate you saw

A finance manager in Lagos needs to pay a supplier in pounds. She checks a rate online, sees a number, and then gets a quote from her bank that is noticeably worse. Nobody lied to her. She compared two different prices without knowing it.

That gap is the spread, and it is the most common place where foreign exchange costs hide. It rarely appears as a line item. It sits inside the rate, which is why so many businesses think they paid no fee when they paid a good deal.

## Mid market, bid and ask

Every currency pair has a mid market rate. It is the midpoint between the price at which dealers are willing to buy a currency and the price at which they are willing to sell it. It is a useful reference. It is not a price anyone can usually trade at.

What you actually face are two numbers. The **bid** is what a dealer pays to buy the base currency from you. The **ask** is what the dealer charges to sell it to you. The ask is always higher than the bid, and the difference between them is the **spread**.

Say the mid rate for a pair is 100. A dealer might quote 99 to buy and 101 to sell. If you buy and then immediately sell back, you lose the width of that gap, even though the market did not move at all. That is a real cost, paid every time you cross.

## Why spreads exist

A spread is not simply greed, though it can include some. It pays for several things at once.

- The risk the dealer carries between taking your trade and offsetting it elsewhere.
- The cost of holding inventory of a currency that may move against them.
- The cost of liquidity, meaning how easily the pair trades at size.
- Operational and compliance costs, which are not small for cross border flows.

Major pairs traded in deep markets tend to have narrow spreads. Pairs involving currencies with thinner markets, tighter capital controls or volatile conditions tend to have wide ones. This is not a judgement on any country. It is what happens when it is harder to find the other side of a trade.

## Spread, fee and margin are three different things

Providers describe their pricing in ways that make comparison hard, so it helps to separate the parts.

The **spread** is the difference between buy and sell prices, or between the mid rate and the rate you are given. The **fee** is a stated charge, flat or percentage, added on top. The **margin** is the provider's markup over what it paid for the currency, which is often how the spread is built.

A provider advertising zero fees may be earning everything through the rate. A provider with a visible fee may be giving you a rate very close to mid market. Neither is automatically better. What matters is the total cost, and you can only see the total by comparing what you send with what arrives.

## How to measure what you really paid

The method is simple and worth doing on every meaningful transfer.

First, note the mid market rate at the time of the transaction. Then take the amount that arrived, add back any stated fees, and work out the effective rate you received. The difference between the effective rate and the mid rate, as a percentage of the mid rate, is your all in cost.

Do this a few times with different providers and the pattern becomes clear. Some are cheap on small transfers and expensive on large ones. Some are good on one corridor and poor on another.

## Where businesses lose money without noticing

Three habits cost more than most teams realise.

**Converting through a middle currency.** Moving naira to pounds through dollars means paying a spread twice. Often it is just how a bank's system routes the trade.

**Treating the first quote as the market.** Spreads vary between providers, and they vary by time of day and by size. A business that always uses one bank out of habit is paying for the convenience, whether it knows it or not.

**Ignoring timing.** Rates move, and a quote that was fair at ten in the morning may be stale by the afternoon. For recurring payments, a business that converts at random moments takes on risk it did not choose. Moving money in a few planned chunks, rather than one large lump at a bad moment, can smooth that out, though it does not remove the risk.

## What a treasury team can do about it

You cannot negotiate the market, but you can negotiate your position within it.

Know your volumes. A business that sends regularly has bargaining power that a one off sender does not, and should ask for pricing tiers, not just accept the standard rate. Ask providers to state their rate as a margin over mid market, so offers can be compared on the same basis.

Keep a simple log: date, pair, amount, mid rate, rate received, fee. After a quarter you will know which provider is cheapest for which job. Treasury tooling should make this automatic, since a number you never see is a number you never manage. That is the thinking behind Isura.

## A habit to take away

Next time you are quoted a rate, ask one question: how does this compare with mid market, and what will arrive at the other end? If the provider cannot answer clearly, that is information too. The spread is not a trick. It is a price, and like any price, it is cheaper to pay when you can see it.

title: A Practical Reading of Nigeria's Data Protection Act for Startups
excerpt: A plain reading of the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 for early stage teams: the ideas that matter, a month one checklist, and where to take proper legal advice.
author: Altisly Strategy Team
content:
## A founder, a spreadsheet and a law

A founder in Lagos runs a lending app. She holds names, phone numbers, BVN related details, transaction history and, because the app asks, a location. A customer emails to ask what data she holds and why. She has no clear answer, and she suspects that is a problem.

It is. This piece is a practical reading of the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 for startups. It is not legal advice, and you should take advice from a qualified Nigerian lawyer for your own case. It is meant to help you ask better questions.

## The shape of the law

The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 sets out how personal data of individuals must be handled, and it created the Nigeria Data Protection Commission as the regulator. Before it, the Nigeria Data Protection Regulation of 2019 filled much of the same ground. The Act places the framework in primary legislation.

The vocabulary will be familiar if you know GDPR, which influenced it. A **data controller** decides why and how personal data is processed. A **data processor** handles it on the controller's behalf. A **data subject** is the person the data is about. Most startups are controllers for their own customers, and processors when they build for someone else.

## The ideas that matter most

**Lawful basis.** You need a legitimate reason to process personal data. The Act lists several, including consent, performance of a contract, a legal obligation and legitimate interests. Consent is the one startups reach for first, and it is often the weakest, because it must be freely given, specific and withdrawable. If you need the data to deliver the service, contract is often the cleaner basis.

**Purpose limitation and minimisation.** Collect what you need for a stated purpose, and use it for that purpose. The location you collected for fraud checks is not automatically available for marketing. If you cannot say why you hold a field, that field is a liability.

**Sensitive data.** Categories such as health, biometrics, religious belief and similar get higher protection. Fintech and health startups handle this more often than they notice. A face scan for identity checks is biometric data.

**Rights of data subjects.** People can ask what you hold, ask for corrections, object to certain uses, and in some cases ask for deletion. You need a way to receive these requests and a habit of answering them, within the time the law allows.

**Security and breach.** You must protect the data with suitable technical and organisational measures. If a breach puts people at risk, the Act expects you to notify the Commission within a short window and, in some cases, the people affected. Check the current timing in the Act and any directions the Commission issues, because details can change.

**Cross border transfers.** Sending data abroad, including to a cloud provider hosted elsewhere, comes with conditions, such as adequate protection in the destination or appropriate safeguards. Many startups transfer data every day without having looked.

**Registration and compliance.** Organisations classed as data controllers or processors of major importance have additional duties, including registration with the Commission and, in some cases, audit filings and a data protection officer. Whether you fall into that class depends on factors set by the Commission, and you should check the current guidance.

## A short working list

Here is what we would do in the first month, in order of return on effort.

- Make a data inventory: what you collect, where it sits, who sees it, why you have it.
- Write a plain privacy notice that matches what you actually do.
- Name a person responsible for data protection, even if it is not their only job.
- Create a route for access and deletion requests, and test it with one real case.
- List every vendor that touches personal data and note where it is hosted.
- Write a one page breach plan: who decides, who calls whom, who writes to the regulator.

None of this needs a large budget. It needs a few honest afternoons.

### Where startups misread it

Two errors recur. The first is treating compliance as a banner: a cookie pop up and a privacy page, with nothing behind them. The second is treating it as a reason to stop: freezing product work until everything is perfect. Neither helps.

The better stance is proportion. Know what you hold. Hold less of it. Protect what remains. Be able to explain all of this to a customer in two paragraphs.

### A hypothetical walk through

Picture a small health savings app. It collects name, phone number, date of birth, a self reported health condition so it can recommend a plan, and a selfie for identity checks. Applying the ideas above:

The health condition and the selfie are sensitive data. The app should ask itself whether it truly needs the condition to sell a savings plan, and if not, stop collecting it. If it does need it, it should say so plainly, explain the purpose, and restrict who can see it.

The selfie is used for identity checks, so the purpose is narrow. That means it should not later be used to train a model for a different feature without a fresh look at the basis for doing so.

The app uses a cloud provider abroad, so it needs to know where the data is stored and what safeguards apply to the transfer. It uses an SMS vendor, so it must know what that vendor does with phone numbers.

Each answer is small. Together they make the difference between a company that can explain itself and one that cannot.

### Contracts with vendors and customers

If you act as a processor for other businesses, as many B2B startups do, your customers will ask for a data processing agreement. It sets out what you may do with their data, how you secure it, how fast you tell them about a breach and what happens when the contract ends. Having a standard version ready saves weeks in a sales cycle.

If you rely on vendors, ask for the same in return. A cloud, analytics or messaging provider is part of your compliance, and what they do with your customers' data remains your responsibility to explain.

## Where the law is still settling

The regulator continues to issue guidance, thresholds and directions, and practice is still forming. Some questions, such as how strictly the Commission will treat transfers to common cloud services, are best answered by current guidance and counsel, not by a blog post.

Start with that inventory. A startup that can answer the question "what do you hold about me, and why?" is already most of the way there.

title: Small Models, Big Wins
excerpt: A small model trained on your own data can beat a large one on speed, cost and predictability. When to choose one, and when not to.
author: Altisly Engineering
content:
A team spends two weeks wiring a large language model into a support tool. It classifies tickets into twelve categories. It works, costs a little more each month than anyone expected, and takes a second or two per ticket. Then someone trains a small model on the company's own labelled tickets. It runs on a modest server, answers in milliseconds, and does the job as well or better.

This keeps happening. Bigger is not always better, and for narrow, repeated tasks, it is often worse.

## What small means

"Small model" is a loose term. We use it for models that are small enough to run cheaply on your own hardware, or even on a phone, and often specialised: a classifier, an embedding model, a compact language model tuned for one job. They sit well below the largest general models in size, and they are not trying to do everything.

## Where they win

**Narrow, high volume tasks.** Routing tickets, detecting language, tagging documents, spotting duplicates, extracting a fixed set of fields. When the task is the same ten thousand times a day, a specialised model is cheaper and faster, and its behaviour is more predictable.

**Latency.** Some products need an answer inside a human blink: autocomplete, live suggestions, fraud checks during a payment. A round trip to a large hosted model often will not fit.

**Cost at scale.** Per request prices look small until volume arrives. A small model on a fixed server turns a variable cost into a flat one.

**Privacy and control.** Running a model inside your own environment means the data does not leave it. For regulated records, that can simplify a long conversation with a compliance team.

**Poor connectivity.** On device models work when the network does not. In markets where data is expensive or patchy, that is a feature users notice.

## Where they lose

Small models are less capable at open ended reasoning, long documents, unusual requests and anything that needs wide general knowledge. Ask a compact classifier something outside its training and it fails without warning.

They also need work. Someone has to gather labelled examples, train or tune, evaluate honestly and maintain the result as the data changes. A large hosted model needs only a prompt. For a first version, or a low volume task, that convenience is worth paying for.

## How we choose

We usually start with a large model, because it lets us learn what the task really is. We write down examples, measure how well it does, and see where the failures cluster.

Then we ask three questions. Is the task narrow enough to name? Is the volume high enough that cost or speed matters? Do we have, or can we cheaply get, labelled examples? If the answer is yes to all three, we try a small model against the large one on the same test set. Often we end up with both: a small model handles the routine ninety percent, and the large one handles the odd cases the small one is unsure about.

That pattern, a cheap first pass with an escalation path, is the most reliable win we have found.

## Be careful with the comparison

Test on your own data, not on a public benchmark. Check performance on the rare, expensive cases as well as the average. And include the full cost: the engineer who maintains the small model is not free.

## Try this next

Pick the single most repeated task your product sends to a large model. Collect a few hundred real examples with correct answers, run both options, and compare accuracy, speed and monthly cost side by side. The result may surprise you in either direction, and either answer is useful.

title: Cash Visibility Is the First Treasury Problem
excerpt: Before forecasting or optimising, a treasury team has to see its cash. Why the picture is blurry, and a practical way to build a trustworthy view.
author: Altisly Studio
content:
Ask a finance director how much cash the company has, and you will often get an answer that begins with "roughly". Roughly, because the balances sit in six bank accounts across three banks, two currencies and a payment processor, and the last time anyone added them up was Tuesday.

That is not a forecasting problem or a strategy problem. It is the first treasury problem: you cannot manage what you cannot see.

## Why the picture is blurry

Cash visibility fails for ordinary reasons.

**Accounts multiply.** A new subsidiary, a new product, a payment provider that holds a balance for you. Each adds a place where money sits, and rarely does anyone remove the old ones.

**Each bank shows its own view.** Different portals, different cut off times, different export formats. Getting one picture means logging into several and copying numbers into a spreadsheet.

**Balances are not the same thing as usable cash.** The ledger balance may include items that have not cleared. Money in a processor wallet is yours but not yet in your bank. A figure that looks comfortable can hide a gap.

**The data is stale on arrival.** A morning spreadsheet is already out of date by lunch, especially when payments can move at any hour.

## What good visibility looks like

You do not need sophistication to start. You need four things.

- One list of every account and wallet the company controls, with an owner for each.
- A balance for each, refreshed at a known time, with the source and timestamp visible.
- A split between ledger balance and available balance where the bank provides it.
- A single view in your reporting currency, with the exchange rate used written beside it.

That is a start. Many companies do not have it.

## How to build it

Start with the inventory, and expect it to surprise you. Ask each team which accounts they use, then compare with what the banks say you hold. The mismatch is the first useful finding, and sometimes includes a dormant account that nobody has looked at in a year.

Next, automate the collection of balances. Banks offer several routes: statement files, reporting through standardised formats, and in some markets APIs. Which is available depends on the bank and country, so ask each one what they provide and how often. Automating even a daily pull removes the copying and the typing errors.

Then pick a rhythm. A daily position by a set time is a good first target. Intraday refreshes can follow, when your payment patterns need them.

Finally, put it where decisions are made. A visibility dashboard that sits in a corner of the finance system, and is looked at once a month, does not change behaviour. Put the balance in front of whoever approves payments.

## What it makes possible, without the fuss

Once you can see cash, other things become possible, and they are much easier. Forecasting starts from real balances. Idle money in one account can cover a shortfall in another, instead of borrowing. Banks can be compared fairly, because you see what each really holds. Approvals get better, because a person can see whether a payment will leave the account short.

None of that works well on top of a blurry picture.

## The caveats

Visibility has a ceiling. You cannot see what banks do not report, and some partners deliver data late or in a poor format. In some countries, access to automated reporting is limited, and manual steps remain. Be honest about which balances are live and which are estimates, and label them.

Do not overbuild at the start either. A well kept spreadsheet fed by a daily statement is better than an elaborate system nobody trusts.

## Start with a list

Open a blank page and write down every account and wallet your company controls, with the balance and the date you last saw it. The act of finishing that list is often the most useful treasury work of the quarter.

title: What Instant Payments Change for Corporate Treasury
excerpt: Instant rails remove the float, the daily cut off and the window to catch mistakes. What corporate treasury teams should change in forecasting, controls and visibility.
author: Altisly Strategy Team
content:
## Friday at 4:55pm

A supplier invoice is due. In the old world, a treasury team could take a view on that: the payment run is Monday, the bank clears it Tuesday, and the money is gone by Wednesday. There was slack in the system, and the slack was useful. It gave people time to check, to chase receivables, and to move cash between accounts.

Instant payment systems remove much of that slack. The change is not only speed. It changes what a treasury team can rely on.

## What instant means here

Instant payment rails let money move between accounts in seconds, at any hour, on any day. Nigeria's NIP is a familiar example for many of our readers, the UK has Faster Payments, and India's UPI is the best known large scale case. They differ in design and rules, but share the property that settlement to the recipient is fast and, typically, final.

Final is the word that matters. A card payment can be disputed, and a cheque can bounce. An instant credit transfer, once sent, is usually very hard to pull back.

## Four things that shift

**The float disappears.** Delay between sending and receiving used to be a quiet source of working capital. Pay on Friday, funds leave on Tuesday. When the money leaves immediately, that buffer is gone, and forecasts built on settlement lags become wrong in a way nobody announced.

**Cash moves outside office hours.** Receipts can land on Saturday night. Payments can leave at 3am. A treasury process that assumes a daily cut off, a morning balance and an end of day position is describing a world that no longer matches the account.

**Mistakes become permanent faster.** A wrong account number in a batch used to leave a window to catch it. Now the window may be a few seconds. Controls such as beneficiary name checks, limits and approvals matter more, and they have to work before the payment, not after.

**Fraud has less time to be noticed.** Fast, final payments suit fraudsters as much as anyone. Business email compromise and fake supplier detail changes are more damaging when the money is gone before anyone reads the email twice.

## What treasury teams can do about it

Treat visibility as the first problem. If you cannot see balances across accounts and banks during the day, you cannot manage cash that moves during the day. Intraday balance reporting, from every bank you use, becomes a basic requirement and not a refinement.

Tighten the approval path for outgoing payments. Dual authorisation, sensible limits by amount and beneficiary, and a hold on any change to payee details until it is confirmed by a second route, such as a call to a known number. These controls cost minutes and save very large mistakes.

Rebuild the forecast. Replace assumptions about settlement lags with actual timing data, and be honest where you do not have it. A shorter, more frequent forecast cycle suits a faster world.

Use the speed on the receiving side. Faster collections are a real benefit. Customers who can pay instantly will often do so, and reconciliation can match the payment to the invoice on the same day if you give each customer a unique reference or virtual account to pay into.

### The other side of the ledger

Instant rails are not a problem to be survived. For many companies they bring faster collection, lower cost of paying out to suppliers and staff, and fewer manual steps. Paying a contractor on the day the work is approved is a better experience for everyone.

But the benefits go to teams whose systems and controls match the rails. Those that keep running batch processes designed for next day settlement will gain little and carry the new risks.

Note, too, that availability differs. Not every bank, country or corridor offers the same speed, and cross border payments are still mostly slower. A treasury team often operates both worlds at once.

### A short note on cross border

Everything above applies most clearly to domestic transfers. Cross border payments remain slower and more varied, with intermediaries, cut off times and compliance checks. Treat them as a separate flow in your forecast and do not assume the speed of the local rail extends to them.

## One thing to do this month

Choose a weekend. Look at what your accounts did over it, and whether anyone on your team knew. If the answer is "nothing happened, or we do not know", that is your starting point, because the rails already run when your team does not.

title: Human in the Loop Is a Design, Not a Disclaimer
excerpt: Saying a person reviews everything is not a control. Reviewers tire, queues win, and approvals become clicks. What it takes to design human oversight that works.
author: Altisly Studio
content:
"A human reviews everything" is one of the most comforting sentences in AI products. It appears in policies, in sales decks, in risk assessments. Often it means that a person somewhere clicks "approve" on a screen, forty times an hour, without time to think.

That is a disclaimer. It moves blame to a person while giving them no real ability to catch a mistake. A genuine human in the loop is something you design.

## Why review decays

People are poor at checking work that is usually right. If the system is correct ninety nine times in a hundred, the reviewer learns to expect correctness. Attention drops. The hundredth case, the one that mattered, goes through with the same quick click as the rest.

This is not laziness. It is how attention behaves under repetition. Aviation and industrial safety have studied the same effect for decades. If you design a review step that depends on constant vigilance, you have designed a step that will fail.

Volume makes it worse. If a reviewer is given the whole queue, the queue wins. They will clear it by approving.

## What a real loop needs

**Show the reviewer why.** An answer alone invites a yes or no. An answer with its source, the fields it relied on and what it was unsure about invites a check. If the reviewer has to rebuild the context from scratch, they will not.

**Route by risk, not by habit.** Not every item deserves a person. Send the low risk, high confidence cases straight through, with sampling to check them, and concentrate people on the cases that are unusual, large or uncertain. Fewer items, closer attention.

**Make disagreement cheap.** If rejecting an output takes five clicks and a free text explanation, people will accept. Give them a fast way to correct, flag or send back, and a way to say why in one tap.

**Authority has to be real.** A reviewer who is judged on throughput is not free to stop the line. The person must have both the time and the standing to say no, and no penalty for doing so often.

**Close the loop.** Corrections should go somewhere useful: into a list of failures the team reviews, into test cases, into changes to the prompts or rules. If feedback vanishes, people stop giving it.

### A hypothetical

Imagine an assistant that drafts replies to customer complaints at a bank. The weak design shows the agent a drafted reply with a "send" button. The stronger design highlights the claims in the draft that depend on account data, shows the data next to them, flags any promise of a refund as needing approval, and passes simple acknowledgements through with a daily sample check by a team lead.

Same model, same people. The second design gets attention where it counts.

## Test the loop itself

You can measure whether review works. Seed the queue with known errors, a few at a time, and see how many are caught. Track how long each review takes, and be suspicious when it drops towards two seconds. Look at the rate at which reviewers change the output. A rate near zero is not good news. It usually means nobody is really looking.

## Where this runs out

There are decisions where review is not enough. If the cost of one error is severe and cannot be undone, a rushed approval is no safeguard and the better answer may be limiting what the system is allowed to do at all. There are also tasks so cheap and so reversible that heavy review costs more than the errors it prevents. Match the weight of the control to the weight of the risk.

## Alert fatigue is the same problem

The same pattern appears wherever a system raises flags that are mostly harmless. Hospital staff learn to tune out alarms that rarely matter. Security teams learn to skim alerts. An AI product that asks a human to confirm every output has created a new alert stream with the same flaw.

The remedy is the same as well: fewer, better flags. A system that interrupts rarely, and is right when it does, earns attention. A system that interrupts constantly trains people to stop listening.

## The next step

Look at one human review step in your product today. Find out how long reviewers actually spend per item, and what fraction they change. Those two numbers will tell you whether you have a loop or a disclaimer.

title: Reconciliation Is Where Fintechs Quietly Fail
excerpt: Nothing crashes when reconciliation fails. The gap just grows until someone asks. Why payment companies lose control of their books here, and how to build matching in from day one.
author: Altisly Studio
content:
## The month end that does not close

At 4pm on the last working day, a finance team is still hunting for 38,000 naira. The bank statement says one number. The ledger says another. The gap is small, the books must close tonight, and three people are scrolling spreadsheets side by side.

This is reconciliation. It is not glamorous, nobody puts it in a pitch deck, and it is where a surprising number of fintechs quietly lose control of their own money.

## What reconciliation is

Reconciliation is the act of proving that two records of the same events agree. Your internal ledger says a customer paid you. The bank, the card processor or the mobile money operator says the money arrived. If both agree, fine. If they do not, something is wrong, and you need to find out what before someone else does.

For a payments company there are usually more than two records. There is your own transaction table, your ledger, the processor's settlement file, the bank statement, and sometimes a partner's report. Each is produced by a different system, at a different time, in a different format.

## Why it fails quietly

Reconciliation breaks in ways that never cause an outage. The product keeps working. Customers keep paying. The gap grows in the background and becomes visible only when somebody looks.

**Timing differences.** A transaction succeeds on Monday, settles on Wednesday and appears on the statement on Thursday. For two days the records legitimately disagree. If your system cannot tell "not yet" from "wrong", every day produces false alarms, and soon the team ignores the alerts.

**Fees and rounding.** Processors deduct fees before settlement. Rates differ by channel. One system rounds each fee, another rounds the total. The differences are tiny, and they are everywhere.

**Duplicates and reversals.** Retries, webhooks delivered twice and chargebacks all create entries that need to be matched to the originals. A reversal that arrives without a clear reference to the first transaction is a puzzle.

**Missing references.** The best matching key is a unique reference passed through every system. When a processor truncates it, or a bank statement drops it, matching falls back to amount and date, which breaks the moment two customers pay the same amount on the same day.

**Manual repair.** When a gap is found, someone fixes it with a journal entry and a note. Enough of those, and the ledger stops being a record of events and becomes a record of corrections.

## What a sound approach looks like

We treat reconciliation as a product, not a month end chore.

First, design for matching from the start. Every transaction carries one internal reference that travels through every external system, and the ledger stores the external reference alongside it. It is cheap to build in and very expensive to retrofit.

Second, reconcile continuously. Run matching daily, or more often, against each source. Small breaks found the next morning are easy to explain. Breaks found a month later are archaeology.

Third, give breaks states. Matched, pending with an expected date, mismatched, and unmatched are different conditions with different owners. A pending item that passes its expected date should turn into an exception on its own.

Fourth, keep corrections visible. Adjustments are separate entries with a reason and an author, never edits to history. That is how you stay auditable.

Finally, make exceptions a queue with an owner. A report that someone may read is not a control. A queue that someone must clear is.

### The honest limits

Perfect matching is not always possible. Some partners send poor data, and some differences are never explained, only written off under a policy your auditors accept. Automation reduces the pile. It does not remove the need for a person who understands the money.

The cost is also real. Building this properly takes engineering time that does not ship a visible feature. Early teams are often right to start with a simple daily match and a clear exception list, and to add sophistication as volume demands it.

### An example of a break, step by step

Suppose a customer pays 50,000 naira to a merchant through your platform. Your system records the payment on Monday. The processor settles to you on Wednesday, deducting a fee of 750 naira, so 49,250 arrives in your bank account. The bank statement shows the credit on Thursday with a truncated narration.

A reconciliation process that works well does the following. On Monday it creates an expected settlement entry marked pending, with an expected date. On Wednesday the settlement file arrives and matches by internal reference, and the fee is recorded as its own line. On Thursday the bank statement credit matches the settlement total, since one credit often covers many transactions. At the end, three records agree, and each step leaves a trace.

Now take the version that fails. The processor settles 49,250, but the narration lost the reference. The statement line cannot be matched. The finance team sees an unexplained credit and a pending payment, and guesses. A guess becomes a manual entry. In a month, it is one of several hundred.

### Who owns this inside a company

In many companies, reconciliation belongs to finance, while the references and data that make it possible belong to engineering. Neither side has the complete picture. Finance sees the breaks and cannot fix their cause. Engineering controls the cause and never sees the break.

The fix is organisational as much as technical. Put one named person in charge of the reconciliation outcome. Give engineering a regular report of the break categories, ranked by cost, so they can remove causes at the source. The best reconciliation teams we know spend their time deleting categories of break, not clearing the same ones every month.

### Signals that your reconciliation is weaker than you think

- Month end close routinely slips because of unexplained differences.
- Write offs are growing, and nobody can say why.
- Only one person understands how the matching spreadsheet works.
- Support tickets about "missing" payments take days to resolve because staff cannot see settlement status.

If two or more are true, it is worth treating this as an engineering project, with a plan and an owner.

## What we would check first

Pick last week. Can you say, for every transaction, whether it matched the bank, and if not, why? If that takes a person three days with a spreadsheet, the weakness is already there. Start with the reference that connects your systems, and build outward from it.

Fintechs rarely fail because a payment button broke. More often it is a gap in the books that nobody could explain in time.

title: The Super App Question in African Markets
excerpt: Investors keep asking when you will become a super app. The Asian model rests on conditions that do not always hold in African markets, and other routes can reach the same value.
author: Altisly Strategy Team
content:
## Every founder gets asked

Sooner or later, a founder building a payments app, a ride service or a marketplace in Lagos, Accra or Nairobi is asked by an investor: "So when do you become a super app?" The question assumes the answer is yes, and that the only matter is timing.

We think the question deserves more suspicion. Super apps are real and some are enormous. But the idea has travelled further than the conditions that produced it.

## What a super app actually is

A super app is a single application that hosts many services: payments, messaging, shopping, transport, food, loans, and often third party mini programs built inside it. The best known examples come from Asia, where one app became the front door for daily life.

Two ingredients tend to sit underneath. First, a very large daily use habit, usually messaging or payments, that people open many times a day. Second, a shared identity and wallet that make adding a new service nearly free for the user. Once someone is verified and has money in the app, ordering a ride is a tap, not a signup.

Everything else follows from those two. The breadth is a consequence, not a plan.

## Why the African case is different

Africa is not one market, so we will be careful. But a few conditions recur across the places we work.

**Fragmented rails.** Bank transfers, mobile money, cards and agent networks coexist, and they differ by country and sometimes by operator. A single wallet that works everywhere is harder to build than it looks, and regulation of stored value varies from one jurisdiction to the next.

**Regulation by activity.** Payments, lending, insurance and investment are licensed separately. A company that adds services also adds regulators. The cost of breadth is not just engineering.

**Existing giants.** In several markets, telecom operators and banks already hold the daily habit and the identity layer. A new entrant is not filling an empty seat.

**Uneven devices and data.** App size, data cost and low end phones all push toward lightweight products. Heavy, do everything apps are a harder sell when storage and bandwidth are precious.

None of this makes super apps impossible. It means the Asian route is not a template.

### Other routes to the same destination

Several shapes compete with the single app, and some suit these markets better.

- **Platform plus partners.** Provide identity, payments and distribution as infrastructure, and let other businesses build the customer facing services. You win by being the thing others depend on, not the thing users open.
- **Embedded services.** Put the financial product inside someone else's flow: a loan at checkout, a wallet inside a logistics app. The user never visits your app. They still use your service.
- **A strong vertical.** Be the best at one job for one kind of business, then widen gradually, because users already trust you there.

Each is a way to capture the value that a super app promises, with less to carry on day one.

## When going broad does make sense

We would consider it if, and only if, there is a genuine daily habit already, not a hoped for one. If people open your app daily for one reason, adding a second reason is cheap. If they open it monthly, adding features just gives them more things to ignore monthly.

It also helps when your shared layer is truly shared. If a new service needs its own onboarding, its own verification and its own wallet, you have built two products under one icon.

### A hypothetical that tests the idea

Picture a payments startup with a wallet, a few hundred thousand users and a good reputation for reliable transfers. Its board asks for a ride hailing feature, a food ordering feature and a bill payments hub, all in one app, within the year.

Each looks small. Ride hailing means drivers, a pricing engine, safety processes and a support operation. Food ordering means restaurants, couriers and disputes. Bill payments means billers, each with its own integration. The wallet, which was the strength, is now one of four businesses the team must run, each with different unit economics. Meanwhile, the competitors in each of those categories do nothing else.

The founders would be better served by asking what the wallet can offer to those businesses as a partner. Let the ride company and the food company accept the wallet at checkout. The company keeps its focus, and the wallet still gains volume.

### What the question hides

The super app question mixes up two ideas: owning the customer relationship and owning every service. They are not the same. A company can own the relationship through identity, a wallet and a trusted brand while others deliver the services. That is closer to what many successful platforms do, and it asks far less of a young company.

It also hides a timing question. Companies that became super apps usually did so after they had won something narrower, and with a large base. Starting from the destination, without the base, tends to produce a thin version of everything.

## Questions that cut through it

Before expanding, ask what the daily action is and who does it. Ask which regulator each new service adds. Ask whether the partner route would reach the same customers with a tenth of the work. And ask whether the pull toward becoming a super app comes from users, or only from a slide in a pitch deck.

Depth tends to make a company hard to leave. Breadth, on its own, usually just makes it hard to run.

title: Structured Output Changed How We Build With LLMs
excerpt: Moving from regexes over free text to schemas changed how we treat models: as typed components we can test, validate and replace. Here is what it fixed and what it does not.
author: Altisly Engineering
content:
## The regex era

Early in building with language models, a lot of our code looked like this: ask the model for a result, receive a friendly paragraph, then write a parser to dig the facts out of it. The parser used regular expressions. The regular expressions were cursed.

Some days the model wrote "Amount: 5,000". Other days "The total is NGN 5000.00". Once it wrote the number in words. Each variation produced a bug, and each bug produced another pattern, until the parsing code was longer than the feature it served.

Structured output ended that. We now think it is one of the most practical changes in how software uses language models, and it deserves less mystique than it gets.

## What it is
