Instead of asking the model to write prose and hoping, you give it a schema: the fields you want, their types, which are required, which values are allowed. The model's response is constrained to match. You receive an object, not a paragraph.

Different providers implement this differently. Some constrain generation directly so that invalid output cannot be produced. Others rely on tool calling, where the schema describes a function the model "calls". The details vary and change over time, so check what your provider guarantees and what it merely encourages. The idea is the same in each case.

A typical schema, written in TypeScript style, might look like this:

```
type InvoiceExtraction = {
  supplier: string
  currency: "NGN" | "GHS" | "GBP" | "USD" | "other"
  amountMinor: number
  dueDate: string | null
  needsReview: boolean
  reviewReason: string | null
}
```

Notice the choices. Money is an integer in minor units, so there is no decimal ambiguity. Currency is an enumeration, so "Naira" and "NGN" cannot both appear. A missing due date is an explicit null, not an invented one.

## What it changed in practice

**The model became a component.** Before, the model was a collaborator whose answers needed interpretation. Now it is a function with a typed return value. Other code can depend on it, test it and replace it.

**Validation moved to the edge.** We still validate the object, because a well formed answer can be a wrong one. But the validator now checks meaning (does the amount make sense, is the date in the future) and not shape. The two kinds of failure are handled differently, and that clarity helps.

**Failures became legible.** When output is free text, a bad result is a mystery. When it is an object, you can see which field was wrong, log it, and count how often. Patterns show up that prose hid.

**Prompts got shorter.** A great deal of old prompt text existed to coax a format: "respond only in JSON, do not add commentary". The schema does that job better, and the prompt can go back to describing the task.

### The habits we have kept

Give the model a way out. Fields like `needsReview` and `reviewReason`, or nullable values, let it say "I am not sure" without inventing something to fill the gap. A schema that forces an answer will get one.

Keep schemas small and specific. One schema per task, with fields that mean one thing each. Large, loose schemas bring the old ambiguity back with better formatting.

Describe the fields. A short description on each property is read by the model and acts as part of the instructions. It is the cheapest accuracy improvement we know.

Version your schemas. Downstream code depends on them, so changing a field is a breaking change, and should be treated as one.

## What it does not fix

A valid object is not a true one. The model can still misread an invoice and return a perfectly shaped, perfectly wrong amount. Structure removes formatting errors, not reasoning errors. Anything that matters, such as money or access, still needs checks that do not trust the model, and often a person for the doubtful cases.

Constrained output can also, in some setups, nudge quality in subtle ways, particularly where the schema forces the model to commit to an answer before it has reasoned. If your task needs thinking first, give the schema a field for reasoning that comes ahead of the answer, and measure the result on your own examples instead of assuming.

### Testing a structured pipeline

Once the output is an object, testing gets ordinary, which is the best thing about it. We keep a set of real inputs with the correct objects beside them, run the pipeline against the set whenever a prompt, schema or model changes, and compare field by field. A change that improves supplier names and quietly worsens due dates is now visible in a single run, where before it would have been a feeling.

Two details help. First, test the awkward inputs on purpose: the blurry scan, the invoice in two currencies, the one with no date. Second, record which cases the model flagged for review, and check that the flagged ones are the ones it really got wrong. A model that is unsure about the right things is more useful than one that is slightly more accurate and confident about everything.

We also keep the schema next to the code that consumes it, so a change to one forces a look at the other. It sounds trivial. It prevents the kind of drift where the prompt promises one shape and the database expects another.

### Cost and speed

Structured output has small costs worth knowing. Schemas add tokens to each request. Strict constraints on generation may add a little latency on the first call with a new schema in some providers. For most workloads this is negligible next to the engineering time saved, but if you run at very high volume, measure it.

## Where to begin

Find the place in your codebase where you parse model output with string handling. Replace that one place with a schema. Keep the old path behind a flag for a week, compare the results, and look at how much code you can delete. In our experience it is more than you expect.

title: Why AI Pilots Stall at the Handoff
excerpt: The demo worked, the model was accurate, and the pilot still never shipped. The failure usually sits where AI output has to become someone's real work.
author: Altisly Strategy Team
content:
The demo went well. The model read the invoice, pulled out the supplier, the amount and the due date, and everyone in the room nodded. Three months later the pilot is "still being evaluated" and nobody can say when it will go live.

We see this pattern often enough to describe it. The model is rarely the problem. The trouble sits at the handoff: the point where the AI's output has to become somebody's actual work.

## The pilot answers the wrong question

A pilot usually asks, can the model do the task? Often it can. But a business does not run on tasks. It runs on a chain of them, and each link has an owner, a system and a deadline.

Take that invoice. Extraction is one step. Someone then has to match it to a purchase order, check it against the budget, route it for approval and post it to the ledger. The AI shortened the first step from four minutes to ten seconds. The other four steps are untouched, and they are where the days go.

If the pilot measures only the step the model handles, it will look like a triumph while the process around it stays exactly as slow as before.

## Three places the handoff breaks

**Nobody owns the output.** The AI produces a result, and then what? In a pilot, a project lead checks it. In production, a finance clerk is meant to, but nobody told her, her queue has not changed, and she does not trust what she did not ask for. Work with no owner does not get done.

**The output does not fit the next system.** A model returns a paragraph. The ledger wants a supplier ID, a currency code and a tax category. Someone ends up retyping, and the saving evaporates. Fit is an engineering problem, and it is dull, which is why it is left until last.

**Errors have nowhere to go.** Models are wrong sometimes. In a demo that is a funny moment. In operations it needs a path: who sees the doubtful ones, how they correct them, and whether the correction improves anything. Without that path, the first visible mistake gets the whole project paused.

## What we do differently

We start from the end of the process, not the beginning. Before choosing a model, we ask where the result lands, who acts on it, and what that person needs to see in order to act without redoing the work.

Then we shape the output for that person and that system. Confidence shown plainly. The source of each extracted value visible beside it. A one click correction. The doubtful cases routed to a named role, and the confident ones passed straight through.

We also change the measure. Not "accuracy of the model" but "time from invoice received to invoice posted". It is a less flattering number, and a truer one.

## Where this advice runs out

Sometimes the handoff is not the problem. The task may be genuinely too hard for current models, or the data too messy, or the volume too low to justify any automation. A pilot that stalls for those reasons should be stopped, and stopping it is a good outcome.

And redesigning a handoff means changing how people work, which is political in a plain, human sense. Someone may lose a task they valued. Say so early.

## A hypothetical from the shop floor

Imagine a distributor that pilots AI to read incoming purchase requests from email. The model does well. But the requests arrive from forty different people, each describing items in their own way, and the stock system accepts only product codes. The pilot team never had to solve that, because they tested on a clean sample. In production, a clerk spends the saved minutes translating the model's answer into codes by hand.

Nothing about the model changed between the demo and the failure. The only thing that changed was that the output met the real process.

## A question for your pilot

Ask who will open the AI's output on a Tuesday afternoon, in a real queue, with real deadlines. If you cannot name the person, you have a demo. Find the person first, and the pilot will have somewhere to go.

title: Patient Records and the Principle of Least Privilege
excerpt: A receptionist should not be able to open every record at every branch. How to design hospital access around role, need and relationship, without slowing clinicians down.
author: Altisly Engineering
content:
## The receptionist who can read everything

Picture a hospital with three branches. A receptionist at one of them opens the patient system to check in a walk in. The same login also lets her open the full record of anyone registered at any branch: diagnoses, lab results, notes from the consultant. She has no reason to look. Nobody has ever told her she cannot.

This is the default state of many hospital systems, and it is rarely a decision. It is what happens when access is built around "staff can log in" instead of "this person needs this thing for this task".

## What least privilege actually says

The principle is old and simple: give each person and each system the minimum access needed to do the job, and no more. In a clinical setting the difficulty is that the job changes by the hour. A nurse covering another ward tonight needs that ward's patients tonight. A billing clerk needs to know a procedure happened, but rarely needs the clinical notes that describe it.

So least privilege in a hospital is not one list of roles. It is three questions asked together:

- **Who** is this, and what is their role at this branch?
- **What** part of the record do they need: demographics, billing, clinical notes, results?
- **Why** now: is this patient assigned to them, or in their queue today?

A role alone answers the first question. Most systems stop there.

## Design choices that make it real

**Separate the parts of a record.** A patient record is not one object. Administrative details, billing, clinical history and sensitive categories each carry different risk. If they live in one blob with one permission, you can only allow everything or nothing. Split them, and a receptionist sees what she needs to register someone and nothing more.

**Tie access to a relationship.** The strongest rule in a clinical system is often "you can open this record because this patient is assigned to you or your ward". It turns access from a standing permission into something earned by the work in front of you. When the assignment ends, so does the access.

**Allow the emergency, then ask about it.** Clinicians sometimes need a record they are not assigned to, and a locked door in an emergency is its own harm. A well designed system lets them break the glass: proceed, give a reason, and know that the access is flagged for review. The friction is small. The accountability is real.

**Log reads, not only writes.** Many systems record who changed something and say nothing about who looked. For patient privacy the looking is the risk. A usable audit trail answers "who viewed this record, when, and from which branch" without a database query and a favour from an engineer.

**Expire temporary access.** Locums, trainees and cover staff are where permissions pile up. Grant access with an end date by default, so removal is the system's job and not somebody's memory.

## Where it does not hold

Least privilege can be pushed too far. If every lookup needs a justification form, staff will share logins to get through the day, and then you have no audit trail at all. The goal is to make the correct path the easy one. A control that slows a nurse during a bad night will be worked around, and rightly so.

There is also a real cost in setup. Defining who needs what takes conversations with clinicians, records officers and administrators, not only engineers. Expect disagreement. Expect the first version to be too tight in places and too loose in others, and plan to adjust it using the audit logs rather than guesses.

Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 treats health data as sensitive personal data, and privacy law in the UK and elsewhere does the same. We would not frame this as a compliance exercise, though. A system that limits access by design is easier to defend, easier to explain to patients, and easier to investigate when something goes wrong.

## A place to start

Pick one question and answer it honestly this week: if a staff member at your smallest branch wanted to read the record of a patient they have never met, what would stop them? If the answer is "nothing, but they would not", you have found your first piece of work. Fix that one thing, and make the audit log show you the next.

title: The Case for Boring Databases
excerpt: New databases arrive with better stories, but most teams should start with PostgreSQL. A case for boring technology, and the signs that it is time to move on.
author: Altisly Engineering
content:
Every few years a new database arrives with a better story than the last one. Faster, more scalable, more flexible, built for the cloud, built for AI. Some of them are excellent. Most teams should still start with PostgreSQL, and many should finish with it too.

That is not a lack of ambition. It is an argument about where a young product spends its limited attention.

## What boring means

A boring database is one whose behaviour is well understood. Its failure modes are documented. Its tools, hosting options, backup methods and monitoring are mature. When something goes wrong at three in the morning, a search finds the answer, because thousands of people have been there before.

PostgreSQL, MySQL and their relatives qualify. They have decades of use behind them. They are not exciting, and that is the point: nobody on your team should be excited by their database during an outage.

## The real price of novelty

Every unusual technology in your stack charges a tax, and the tax is paid in attention.

Someone must learn its quirks. Someone must work out how to back it up and, more importantly, how to restore it. Someone must understand how it behaves under load, what consistency it actually offers and what happens during a network partition. Hiring becomes harder because fewer people know it. Tooling is thinner. Documentation may be incomplete or out of date.

A new database may well be better at one thing. But you adopt all of it, including the parts that are merely different. Early in a company's life, the scarce resource is not query speed. It is the time of the few engineers who have to keep everything running while also building the product.

## Boring is more capable than its reputation

A common reason for reaching for something specialised is a belief that a relational database cannot do the job. Often it can.

- **Documents.** PostgreSQL has a JSON type, `jsonb`, that can be indexed and queried. Teams that wanted flexible schemas often discover they can have a relational core and a flexible column in the same system.
- **Search.** Built in full text search handles many needs before a dedicated search engine is justified.
- **Queues.** A table with careful locking can serve as a job queue for moderate volumes. Row level locking features such as `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` exist for exactly this pattern.
- **Time series and geospatial work.** Extensions extend the same engine into these areas.
- **Transactions.** This is the big one. Being able to change several related records atomically, with the database enforcing constraints, removes whole classes of bugs that otherwise land in application code.

Here is a small example of the queue pattern, to show how ordinary it is:

```
SELECT id, payload
FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'pending'
ORDER BY created_at
LIMIT 10
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
```

It will not suit every workload, but for a lot of products it removes a whole separate system.

Operations deserve a mention of their own. A mature database has well worn answers to the questions that decide whether you sleep at night. Point in time recovery lets you restore to just before a bad deployment. Streaming replication gives you a standby. Managed hosting from the large cloud providers handles patching and backups, and a competent engineer can learn the essentials in days. Compare that with a young system where the recovery procedure is a forum thread from last month.

Schema discipline is a quiet advantage too. A relational schema forces you to decide what your data is. Constraints, foreign keys and types catch mistakes at write time, rather than letting them surface as odd behaviour months later. Teams that skip this often rebuild it, badly, in application code.

Migrations are easier to reason about as well. Changing a column in a database you understand is a known procedure with known risks.

## Fewer systems, fewer problems

Each additional data store is another thing to secure, back up, monitor, upgrade and keep consistent with the others. When the same fact lives in two systems, you now have a synchronisation problem, and synchronisation bugs are some of the hardest to diagnose.

One well run database gives you one source of truth, one backup story, one place to enforce rules about money, identity and permissions. For software that handles financial records or patient data, that simplicity is not a nicety. It is part of being able to explain to an auditor what is true.

## When boring stops being enough

This is not a claim that specialised databases are pointless. They exist because real workloads outgrow general tools.

You may genuinely need something different when your data volume or write rate is beyond what a single well tuned relational setup can handle, when your access pattern is unusual in a way the engine cannot model, such as deep graph traversal at scale, or when latency requirements demand an in memory store. Analytical workloads over very large datasets are often better served by a columnar warehouse than by the database running your application.

The crucial point is sequence. Reach for the specialised tool when you have measured a problem the general one cannot solve, not when you have imagined one. Premature scale is an expensive hobby.

A final practical point: boring does not mean neglected. Run the database well. Index for your real queries, watch slow query logs, test restores on a schedule and keep it upgraded. Most complaints that a relational database cannot scale turn out to be complaints about a missing index or an untested query.

## How to decide

Before adding a data store, ask these questions:

- What specific requirement does this meet that our current database cannot?
- Have we measured it, or are we guessing?
- Who on the team can operate it, restore it and debug it at night?
- What happens to consistency between this and our main database?

If those have good answers, go ahead. If the honest answers are vague, the reason is probably fashion.

## A closing thought

Choose the database that lets you stop thinking about the database. Spend the saved attention on the part of your product that customers actually notice, and revisit the choice when real numbers, not forecasts, tell you to.

title: Quantum Computing for People Who Ship Software
excerpt: What a quantum computer can and cannot do, what to ignore in the headlines, and the one area, cryptography, where ordinary engineers should act sooner.
author: Altisly Engineering
content:
## A fair question from a busy engineer

You ship software for a living. Every few months a headline announces a quantum breakthrough, and a colleague asks whether you should be worried, excited or retraining. The honest answer is neither, for most of us, today. But there is one part that deserves attention now, and the rest is worth understanding at a sensible level so you can ignore the noise.

## What a quantum computer is, without the mysticism

A classical computer works with bits, each either 0 or 1. A quantum computer works with qubits, which can be in combinations of states described by quantum mechanics. Operations on many qubits can be arranged so that certain wrong answers cancel out and right answers reinforce, a property called interference.

That does not mean a quantum computer tries every answer at once and picks the best one. That popular description is misleading. The machine is not faster at everything. It is useful for specific kinds of problems where the structure lets interference do real work.

Think of it less as a faster laptop and more as a specialised instrument, closer to a very unusual accelerator.

## What it is good at, as far as we know

The problems with strong theoretical backing are narrow.

- **Factoring large numbers and related problems.** Shor's algorithm, published in the 1990s, shows that a large enough quantum computer could factor integers efficiently, which matters because much of today's public key cryptography relies on that being hard.
- **Simulating quantum systems.** Molecules and materials obey quantum rules, and simulating them classically gets very expensive. This is a natural fit and an area of serious research interest in chemistry and materials science.
- **Some search and optimisation tasks.** Grover's algorithm offers a quadratic speed up for unstructured search, which is useful but not dramatic. Claims about quantum computers solving every optimisation problem outright are not established.

For ordinary business workloads, such as running a web application, processing payments, serving a database or training most machine learning models, there is no known quantum advantage.

## Where the hardware actually is

Today's machines are small and error prone. Qubits are fragile and lose their state quickly, so useful computation requires error correction, which in turn needs many physical qubits to make one reliable logical qubit. Building machines large and stable enough to run something like Shor's algorithm on cryptographically relevant numbers is a hard engineering challenge, and nobody can say with confidence exactly when it will be met.

Be sceptical of any claim that gives a firm date, in either direction. Progress is real, and so is the distance still to cover.

## The part that matters to you now: cryptography

Here is why this reaches ordinary engineers. Data encrypted today can be recorded and stored by an adversary who hopes to decrypt it later, once a capable quantum computer exists. This is often described as harvest now, decrypt later. For information that must stay confidential for many years, such as health records, financial history or state secrets, that risk is relevant before the machines arrive.

The response is post quantum cryptography: algorithms designed to resist both classical and quantum attacks. The US standards body NIST ran a multi year public process and has published standards for several such algorithms. Standards bodies and governments have begun issuing guidance for migrating.

Symmetric encryption such as AES is considered much less affected, since the known quantum speed up is modest and can be countered with larger key sizes. The main concern is public key systems used for key exchange and digital signatures.

## What you can practically do

You do not need to rewrite anything this quarter. Sensible steps are modest.

Take inventory. Find where your systems use cryptography: TLS, VPNs, signed tokens, stored data, hardware devices. You cannot migrate what you cannot list.

Build crypto agility. Avoid hard coding algorithms and key sizes deep in your code. If swapping an algorithm means a rewrite, you will be slow when you need to move.

Watch your vendors and libraries. Many will add post quantum options on their own schedule, and mainstream TLS stacks have begun experimenting with hybrid approaches that combine classical and new algorithms.

Prioritise long lived secrets. Data with a long confidentiality life deserves earlier attention than session traffic that is worthless next week.

A word on the hype around quantum and AI together. Some claims suggest quantum machines will soon transform machine learning. There is research interest, but no established general advantage, and loading data into a quantum computer is itself a hard problem. Treat the pairing as an open research question, not a roadmap.

Another common confusion is between quantum computing and quantum communication. The latter, including quantum key distribution, uses quantum effects to exchange keys. It needs specialised hardware and has limited practical reach, and most organisations will rely on post quantum algorithms in software instead.

It also helps to know the vocabulary of the hardware race. Different approaches exist, including superconducting circuits, trapped ions and photonics, each with trade offs in stability and scale. You do not need to pick a winner. You only need to know that headline qubit counts are not comparable between them, because quality of qubits matters as much as quantity.

## What to ignore

Ignore claims that quantum computing will make your product obsolete, that it will soon break all encryption overnight, or that you need a quantum strategy before you have a cryptography inventory. Also ignore the opposite claim that it is all hype. The field has a solid scientific basis and some real consequences.

One more practical note: be wary of consultants who sell a quantum readiness programme in the abstract. A good first deliverable is a simple list of your cryptographic dependencies and their owners, and that can be produced by your own team in a few weeks.

## Where we land

For people who ship software, quantum computing is a slow moving infrastructure concern, not a product opportunity. Learn enough to explain it plainly, get your cryptography in order, and revisit the question when the evidence changes. That is a modest plan, and for most teams it is the right size.

title: Election Technology: Why Transparency Beats Speed
excerpt: Election results arrive faster with technology, but trust depends on whether a sceptic can check them. The design properties that matter more than speed.
author: Altisly Studio
content:
## The race to the result

On the night of an election, the pressure is almost always about speed. Citizens want results, media want them sooner, and officials feel the weight of both. Technology is often introduced with a promise to deliver results faster. That promise is easy to make and easy to measure.

It is also the wrong thing to optimise first. An election is not a computation whose value is the answer. It is a process whose value is that the losing side can accept the answer. That depends on trust, and trust depends on being able to check.

## What speed cannot buy

A fast result that people doubt is worse than a slower one they believe. Doubt is costly: it fuels disputes, litigation and sometimes unrest, and it lingers long after the count is finished.

Technology can make errors faster and less visible too. A paper count has a human scale: observers stand in a room and watch ballots being sorted. A digital system can fail silently, in software that few people can inspect, and a single flaw can affect many results at once. Speed amplifies whichever way a system fails.

So the design question is not how quickly can we count, but how can everyone with a legitimate interest verify that the count is right.

## Properties worth designing for

This is a discussion about design, not about any party or candidate. A few properties recur in serious thinking about voting systems.

- **Verifiability.** Can a voter, an observer or an auditor confirm that votes were recorded and counted as cast? Systems that leave a durable, voter checked record, such as a paper trail, make independent checks possible.
- **Auditability.** Can results be checked after the fact against independent evidence? Post election audits, where a sample of paper records is compared with electronic totals, are one widely used method.
- **Transparency of results.** Publishing results at polling unit level lets anyone add them up and compare with the total. Aggregated numbers alone ask people to take the centre's word.
- **Secrecy.** Voters must be able to cast ballots privately, and nobody should be able to prove how someone voted. This sits in tension with verifiability, and good designs manage the tension carefully.
- **Resilience.** Power, connectivity and logistics fail. A system that works only in perfect conditions will not survive election day.
- **Access.** Voters with disabilities, limited literacy or no technical experience must be able to use it unaided.

## Where technology helps

None of this is an argument against technology. Electronic tools can reduce clerical errors in compiling results, help manage voter registers, speed up logistics and publish detailed results to the public in open formats. Digital transmission of results from polling units can be paired with the original signed paper forms, so that each backs up the other.

The pattern that holds up is technology as an aid to a process that stays checkable, rather than technology as a replacement for checks.

Consider a hypothetical country that moves results transmission online. If every polling unit result sheet is also photographed and published, citizens and observers can compare the digital figure with the signed paper. A mismatch becomes visible and fixable. Without that, a mismatch becomes a rumour.

Timing matters as well. Rules about when results are final, how disputes are heard and what evidence is kept should be settled well before the vote. Designing them on the night, under pressure, is how suspicion grows.

## Open processes beat clever ones

Transparency is not only about results. It extends to how systems are procured, tested and certified. Independent testing, published procedures, public demonstrations and access for accredited observers all give people reasons to believe the machinery. Where software is concerned, independent review of how it works builds more confidence than assurances from the vendor.

Complexity is itself a risk. Every added layer is another place for something to go wrong and another thing observers must understand. A simpler process that people grasp can be more trustworthy than a sophisticated one they must take on faith.

Public understanding is part of the design too. If citizens cannot explain, in a sentence or two, how their vote becomes a number on a screen, suspicion has room to grow. Civic education before polling day, plain language guides and open demonstrations of the equipment cost little next to the price of a disputed result.

## A fair test

When evaluating any election technology, ask whether a sceptical but reasonable person, with no stake in the outcome, could check the result without trusting the people who produced it. If so, speed is a welcome bonus. If not, speed is just a faster way to lose confidence.

title: Who Answers for the Algorithm? Accountability in Automated Decisions
excerpt: When an automated system declines a loan or filters a job application, someone must answer for it. What accountability looks like in design, records and review.
author: Altisly Studio
content:
## When the computer says no

Someone applies for a loan and is declined within seconds. A job application is filtered out before a person sees it. A payment is flagged and an account frozen. In each case the applicant asks the same question: why? And in too many organisations, nobody in the building can answer.

Automated decisions are not new, but they are spreading into places where the stakes are high and the reasoning is opaque. The question that follows is practical, not philosophical: when such a system gets it wrong, who is answerable?

## The temptation to blame the model

It is easy to treat an algorithm as an independent actor. The system decided. The model scored. This framing is convenient because it spreads responsibility so thinly that nobody holds it.

It does not survive scrutiny. People chose to deploy the system, chose its training data, chose the threshold at which a score becomes a refusal, and chose whether anyone reviews the outcome. Each of those is a human decision with an owner, even if the owner has not been named.

A useful rule is that an organisation cannot outsource accountability to software. If a firm uses an automated tool to make decisions about people, the firm answers for those decisions, whoever built the tool.

## What the law already says

Regulators have started to codify this, and the direction is consistent even where details differ. The GDPR, in force since May 2018, gives people certain rights concerning decisions based solely on automated processing that significantly affect them, including safeguards such as the ability to obtain human intervention and to contest the decision. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 also contains provisions on automated decision making. The EU AI Act, which entered into force in August 2024 with obligations phasing in over time, takes a risk based approach and places requirements such as human oversight and documentation on systems classed as high risk.

Anyone operating in these markets should read the actual texts and take legal advice on how they apply, since scope and exceptions matter. The design lesson, though, is stable: regulators expect explanation, oversight and a route to challenge.

## Building accountability into the system

Accountability is not a policy document. It is a set of features and habits.

- **A named owner.** Every automated decision process should have a person or role responsible for its outcomes, reachable by affected people.
- **Records.** Log the inputs, the version of the model or rules, the result and any human intervention. Without this, an explanation after the fact is guesswork.
- **Explanations people can use.** Not the maths, but the main reasons in plain language, and what the person could do differently.
- **Meaningful human review.** A person who rubber stamps every machine output is not oversight. Reviewers need time, authority and enough information to disagree.
- **A route to challenge.** A clear way to contest a decision, with a human answer and a deadline.
- **Monitoring.** Track outcomes across groups and over time. Systems drift, and unfair patterns often show up in aggregates before anyone complains.

Take a hypothetical lender that uses an automated score to approve small business loans. If the cut off is set too high, deserving applicants are refused in large numbers. Someone chose that cut off. Someone decided whether declined applicants could ask for a second look. Naming those people in advance turns a vague worry into a manageable responsibility.

## The honest limits

None of this makes automation safe by itself. Some models are hard to explain faithfully. Some decisions involve trade offs where reasonable people disagree about what is fair. Human reviewers can be biased too, and sometimes a consistent algorithm is better than inconsistent people. The goal is not to prove machines worse, but to make sure that whichever approach is used, someone can be asked why.

## A question to ask before deploying

Imagine the worst case: a person harmed by a wrong decision arrives at your door. Can you tell them what happened, who is responsible, and how to put it right? If the answer is no, the system is not ready, however accurate its test results look.

title: Feature Flags Are Debt With Interest
excerpt: Feature flags make shipping safer, then quietly pile up as dead code. Treat each one as a loan with an owner and a repayment date.
author: Altisly Engineering
content:
A feature flag is a small thing. One conditional, one switch, a safe way to ship code without showing it to anyone. That is exactly why teams add them so freely, and why, a year later, nobody can say which ones are still doing anything.

## Why flags are worth having

Flags separate deploying code from releasing it. You can merge unfinished work behind a switch, turn a feature on for staff first, roll it out to a fraction of users, and switch it off in seconds if something breaks. For teams shipping often, that is a genuine safety mechanism. We use them and would not give them up.

The trouble is that the benefit arrives on day one and the cost arrives slowly.

## Where the interest accrues

Every flag is a fork in the code. Two paths exist where one used to, and both need to keep working. With one flag that is trivial. With twenty, the number of possible combinations is enormous, and nobody has tested most of them.

Costs compound in familiar ways:

- **Testing.** Each live flag multiplies the states your tests should cover. In practice teams test the default and hope.
- **Reading the code.** A function wrapped in three conditionals about launches that finished long ago is hard to reason about. New engineers cannot tell which branch is real.
- **Stale flags.** A switch that has been on for everybody for eight months is no longer a switch. It is dead code with a name, and removing it later feels risky because the reason for it is forgotten.
- **Incidents.** Changing a flag in production is a deployment of sorts, often with less review than code. A flag flipped to fix one thing can break another, and the config change may not show in the usual history.

## Not all flags are the same

Much of the confusion comes from treating different things as one. It helps to name the kinds:

**Release flags** hide unfinished work. They should be short lived. Once the feature is fully launched, the flag has done its job.

**Experiment flags** split users to compare variants. They end when the experiment concludes.

**Operational flags**, sometimes called kill switches, let you disable a risky or expensive feature under load. These can legitimately live for years, but they should be few and documented.

**Permission flags** gate features by plan or customer. These are really product configuration and belong in a proper entitlement system, not in the same pile as temporary toggles.

When these share one mechanism and one naming style, nobody knows which are meant to expire.

## Paying it down

The fix is mostly habit, not tooling.

Give every flag an owner and an expected removal date when it is created. Put it in the ticket, in the code comment, or in the flag system if it supports that. A flag without an owner is a future mystery.

Make removal part of the definition of done. A feature is not finished when it ships to everyone; it is finished when the flag and the old path are deleted. Schedule that cleanup as real work, in the same sprint where possible.

Review the list regularly. A short monthly look at which flags have been fully on or fully off for weeks will find most of the dead ones. Some teams add a build warning or a test that fails when a flag outlives its date.

Keep the number of simultaneous flags low enough that someone could explain them all. If that is no longer true, stop adding and start deleting.

## The test we use

Before adding a flag, ask: when will this be gone, and who will remove it? If there is no answer, the flag is not a safety measure. It is a loan with no repayment date, and the interest is paid by whoever reads that code next.

title: The Pharmacy Inventory Problem
excerpt: Medicines have batches and expiry dates, which makes pharmacy stock harder than ordinary retail. Why the count drifts, and what a trustworthy inventory system does differently.
author: Altisly Studio
content:
## The shelf that lies

A pharmacist is asked for a common medicine. The system says there are forty units in stock. The shelf has twelve. Or the shelf has plenty, but the batch at the front expires next month while a fresher batch sits behind it. Either way, someone has to guess, and in a pharmacy a guess has consequences that a shortage of stationery never does.

Pharmacy inventory looks like ordinary stock control. It is harder, for reasons worth understanding before choosing or building a system.

## What makes it different

Most retail stock is interchangeable: one tin of tomatoes is the same as another. Medicines are not. Each unit belongs to a batch, and each batch has an expiry date, a supplier and sometimes storage requirements. Two boxes of the same product can have very different value to the pharmacy, because one may have six months of life left and the other six weeks.

So the real unit of inventory is not the product but the product in a batch. A system that tracks only totals cannot tell you what is about to become waste, or which batch to dispense first.

Other differences add up:

- **Expiry is a hard deadline.** Expired stock cannot be sold or dispensed. It is a pure loss, and in some settings it must be disposed of in a documented way.
- **Some medicines are controlled.** They require stricter records of who received what, in what quantity, with reconciliation that matches the register.
- **Demand is lumpy.** Seasonal illness, a clinic's prescribing habits or a single large prescription can swing consumption.
- **Supply is unreliable.** In many markets, stock-outs and delayed deliveries are routine, which tempts pharmacies to over order and then hold stock that ages.

## The failures we see in principle

Three patterns recur wherever inventory is managed loosely.

First, the count drifts away from reality. Stock is dispensed without being recorded, or received without being checked in. The system number becomes folklore, and staff stop trusting it, which accelerates the drift.

Second, expiry is found by accident. Without batch level visibility, the only way to discover short dated stock is to walk the shelves. Things get missed.

Third, ordering is by instinct. Reorder decisions based on memory lead to both shortages and surplus, often in the same week.

## What a good system does

Receiving should capture batch number and expiry at the door, when the box is in hand. Dispensing should suggest the batch that expires first, a rule often called first expiry, first out. Stock counts should be quick enough to do regularly, in small cycles by shelf or category, rather than a dreaded annual exercise.

Alerts should be few and meaningful: items nearing expiry within a window the pharmacy chooses, items below a reorder level that reflects real consumption, and discrepancies between counts and records. Reports should help a pharmacist decide what to order, what to return to suppliers where terms allow, and what to move between branches.

For hospital pharmacies, linking dispensing to the prescription and the patient record closes the loop. Stock leaves because something was prescribed, and that link is what makes discrepancies explainable.

## Start simple, stay honest

Barcode scanning reduces typing and errors, but only if products and batches are scanned consistently. A modest system used every day beats an elaborate one used when convenient. Begin with accurate receiving and dispensing, add regular cycle counts, and let the data show you where the waste actually is. Trust in the number is the real asset, and everything else follows from it.

title: Designing for the Consultation Room
excerpt: A consultation lasts minutes and the software either supports it or competes with it. Here is how to design hospital systems around the conversation, not just the record.
author: Altisly Studio
content:
## Two people and a screen

A consultation room has three participants: the clinician, the patient and the computer. In many hospitals, the computer wins the attention contest. The doctor types while the patient talks, eyes drift to the monitor, and the person describing their worry ends up addressing the side of a head.

This is not a failing of doctors. It is a design problem, and it is one that people who build hospital software can do something about.

## Start with the ten minutes, not the data model

Hospital systems are usually designed around records: what must be captured, billed, reported. That is necessary. But the consultation is a short, pressured conversation, and the interface either supports it or competes with it.

Picture a clinic with a queue in the corridor and a ten minute slot per patient. In that time the clinician has to review history, listen, examine, decide, explain, prescribe and document. Every extra click or screen load comes out of the part that actually matters. A form that demands fifteen mandatory fields before a note can be saved teaches clinicians to fill them with whatever gets them through.

So we start by watching the consultation itself, or hearing it described, and ask what the clinician needs at each moment. Before: a clear summary of the last visit, current medications, allergies and recent results. During: fast entry that does not break eye contact. After: orders and a note that reflect what was decided, with little retyping.

## Principles that hold up

- **Show what matters first.** Allergies and active medications should not sit three tabs deep. Safety information belongs where it cannot be missed.
- **Capture once.** If a vital sign was recorded at triage, the doctor should see it, not re enter it. Duplicate entry is the classic source of both frustration and error.
- **Make common things quick.** The most frequent diagnoses, prescriptions and orders should take a couple of taps. Rare cases can be slower.
- **Allow structure without forcing it.** Free text is how clinicians think. Structured fields are how reports and billing work. Good design lets people write naturally and still produces usable data, rather than demanding one at the expense of the other.
- **Fail gracefully.** Power cuts and weak connectivity are normal in many facilities. A screen that freezes mid consultation is worse than none. Offline friendly design, with saved drafts and sync when the connection returns, is not a luxury in our markets.

Think about a follow up visit. The clinician opens the record and needs three things within seconds: what was decided last time, what has changed since, and what is outstanding. If the answer sits in a scrolling wall of notes, the clinician skims, and skimming is where details are lost. A short, structured summary at the top, drawn from the earlier note, does more for safety than another alert.

The same goes for orders. Requesting a test or writing a prescription should feel like part of the conversation, not a separate administrative task done afterwards. When it happens in the room, with the patient watching, mistakes are more likely to be caught on the spot.

## The patient is a user too

The patient rarely sees the interface, but they feel it. Screen sharing, where the clinician turns the monitor so the patient can see a result or a medication list, builds understanding. Clear printed or messaged instructions after the visit help the patient follow a plan. A system that speaks only to billing departments leaves the patient with nothing.

Language and literacy matter here as well. Instructions in plain wording, and where relevant in the languages patients actually speak, reduce confusion.

## Be careful with clever features

Prompts and alerts can help, but too many of them train people to click through. Alert fatigue is well documented in clinical settings: when every screen warns about something, warnings stop being read. We would rather show fewer, better targeted prompts than a constant stream, and test them with the people who will see them.

Any feature touching clinical decisions should be reviewed by clinicians and governed by the hospital's own protocols. Software should support judgement, not quietly replace it.

## How to find out if it works

Sit in. Time a consultation with the old process and the new. Ask clinicians what they stopped doing and what they started working around, because workarounds are the most honest feedback a system gets. Revisit the design after a month of real use, when habits have formed.

The best measure of a consultation room system is how little of the consultation it takes.

title: Passkeys and the Slow End of Passwords
excerpt: Passkeys remove the secret that attackers steal, which is why they may finally replace passwords. The slow part is recovery, device spread and the legacy systems still asking for eight characters.
author: Altisly Engineering
content:
Passwords have been dying for as long as most engineers have been working. Every year someone declares the end, and every year a login form still asks for eight characters, one capital and a symbol. Passkeys are the first replacement that has a realistic chance of changing that, and the reason is not cleverness. It is that they remove the thing attackers actually steal.

## What a passkey is

A passkey is a credential based on public key cryptography, built on the WebAuthn and FIDO2 standards. When you register, your device creates a key pair. The private key stays on the device, or in a synced credential store, and the public key goes to the service. To sign in, the service sends a challenge, your device signs it after you unlock it with a fingerprint, face or device PIN, and the service checks the signature.

Nothing secret crosses the network. There is no shared password for the service to leak, because the service only holds a public key. A breached database yields nothing an attacker can replay on its own.

## Why this beats the alternatives

The usual weakness of passwords is not that people choose poor ones, though they do. It is that a password can be typed into the wrong place. Phishing works because the user hands the secret to a convincing fake.

Passkeys are bound to the real website's domain. A fake page on a lookalike address simply cannot get a valid signature from the device, because the credential will not respond to the wrong origin. The user does not have to spot the trick. The protocol does it for them.

Compare this with common second factors. Text message codes can be intercepted or socially engineered through SIM swaps. One time codes from an app can be typed into a phishing page and relayed in real time. Passkeys avoid both problems, and they are also faster for the user: one touch, no code to copy.

## Why it is still slow

If the technology is better, why are passwords still everywhere? Mostly because of the unglamorous parts.

- **Recovery.** What happens when someone loses their phone? Every account system needs a recovery path, and attackers aim at the weakest one. If you replace a strong login with an easily abused "forgot access" flow, you have gained nothing.
- **Device spread.** Passkeys sync through platform providers such as Apple, Google and Microsoft, and through some password managers. Moving between ecosystems has improved but is not frictionless, and users on shared or older devices struggle.
- **Awareness.** Many users do not know what a passkey is. Prompts that say "create a passkey" mean little to someone who simply wants to check a balance.
- **Legacy systems.** Banks, hospitals and government portals run software that predates these standards. Retrofitting is slow and carries risk.

In markets like Nigeria and Ghana, where many users share devices, use low cost Android phones, or change numbers often, these frictions are sharper. A passkey strategy that assumes everyone owns a recent personal smartphone will exclude people.

## What we would do as builders

Treat passkeys as an addition first. Offer them alongside existing login, encourage adoption at moments when the user is already authenticated, and let the old method fade as usage grows. Forcing a switch before recovery is solid is how support queues explode.

Design recovery as carefully as sign in. That means verified contact details, a second registered device where possible, and for high value accounts, a deliberate and slower process that involves identity checks. Make it hard for an attacker to talk their way in.

Keep sensitive actions behind fresh authentication. A passkey login is strong, but transferring money or changing payout details should still ask for confirmation at the point of action.

Finally, write the copy for humans. "Sign in with your fingerprint or face" lands better than technical vocabulary.

## What to expect

Passwords will not vanish. They will become the fallback that most users rarely touch, then the one they forget they have. That is a slow end, but a real one, and for any team building a login screen today, designing for passkeys is already the sensible default.

title: Stablecoins in Cross Border B2B Payments: Promise and Limits
excerpt: Stablecoins can speed up the movement of value between two points. They do not remove conversion, compliance or controls, which is where cross border business payments actually get hard.
author: Altisly Strategy Team
content:
## A payment that should not take four days

A manufacturer in Lagos pays a supplier abroad. The money leaves a naira account, passes through a correspondent bank, gets converted somewhere along the way, and arrives days later minus fees nobody quoted at the start. The finance team does not know exactly when it will land or exactly how much will arrive. This is the ordinary experience of cross border business payments, and it is why stablecoins attract serious attention from treasurers, not only from speculators.

The attention is deserved, up to a point. The point is worth locating carefully.

## What a stablecoin actually is

A stablecoin is a digital token designed to hold a steady value, usually by being backed one for one by reserves such as cash or short term government securities, or by other mechanisms. The best known ones track the US dollar. Because they move on public blockchains, they can be sent between wallets at any hour, any day, without a bank being open.

That last property is the whole appeal. Settlement can be fast and continuous, and the cost of moving value across borders can be low compared with traditional correspondent chains. For a business paying overseas suppliers, or receiving dollars from foreign customers, the pitch is simple: skip the slow middle.

## Where the promise is real

There are genuine strengths, and it would be dishonest to wave them away.

- **Speed and availability.** A transfer does not wait for banking hours or for a chain of intermediaries to each process it.
- **Predictability.** When you send a dollar token, the amount the recipient gets is clearer than in a multi hop wire where each bank may deduct something.
- **Access to a dollar like asset.** In economies with currency volatility or tight foreign exchange availability, holding a dollar denominated balance is attractive to businesses as well as individuals.
- **Programmability.** Payments can be tied to conditions, such as release on delivery, in ways that ordinary bank rails do not easily support.

For some corridors and some businesses, these benefits are practical, not theoretical.

## Where it stops being simple

The difficulty is that moving the token is the easy part. Business payments are surrounded by things the token does not solve.

**On and off ramps.** Your supplier does not want tokens, they want money in a bank account. Somebody has to convert naira to the stablecoin at one end and the stablecoin to local currency at the other. Those conversions carry spreads, fees and counterparty risk, and the quality of the ramp often matters more than the quality of the token. A fast blockchain transfer sandwiched between two slow, expensive conversions is not a fast payment.

**Regulation.** Rules differ by country and keep changing. Some jurisdictions have built licensing regimes for stablecoin issuers and service providers. Others restrict or discourage crypto asset activity for businesses and banks. In Nigeria, the position of regulators on digital assets has shifted over the years, and any company planning to use them for trade payments needs current legal advice, not a blog post. The same applies in the UK and Ghana, where the frameworks are different again.

**Reserve and issuer risk.** A stablecoin is only as stable as the reserves and governance behind it. Holders depend on the issuer's ability to redeem at par. Reserve quality, transparency, and legal claims in a failure all matter, and they vary between issuers. Some stablecoins have lost their peg in the past. A treasurer should treat the issuer as a counterparty and assess it like one.

**Accounting, tax and audit.** Your auditors need to know how to classify a token balance. Your tax adviser needs to know when a conversion creates a taxable event. Your bank may ask questions about the source of funds. These are solvable, but they are work.

**Compliance.** Anti money laundering and sanctions checks apply to business payments however they move. Moving value on a public ledger does not exempt anyone from knowing who they are paying and why. In practice, screening and record keeping become more important, not less, because a regulator can see the trail.

A useful habit is to price the whole journey, not the leg that moves on a blockchain. Ask what the supplier receives in their own bank account, in their own currency, and how long it took from the moment you approved the payment.

## The operational side is where businesses get hurt

Most trouble in practice is mundane. Wrong network selected, so funds go to an address that cannot receive them. Wallet keys held by one person who then leaves. A payment approved by one signature because the wallet tooling had no approval workflow. Reconciliation that depends on matching a blockchain transaction hash to an invoice by hand.

Treasury controls that exist for bank payments, such as segregation of duties, dual approval, limits and audit trails, need to exist here too. A token transfer is irreversible. There is no recall message to the bank. That makes pre payment validation and approval policy more valuable, not less.

## A sensible way to approach it

We would not tell a business to avoid stablecoins, and we would not tell it to rush in. A measured path looks like this:

- Pick one corridor and one use case, with a payee who is willing and able to receive this way.
- Use regulated, reputable providers for conversion and custody rather than assembling the pieces yourself.
- Compare the total landed cost with your current method, including ramp spreads and staff time, not only the network fee.
- Write down the control policy before the first payment: who approves, what limits apply, how records are kept.
- Keep your bank relationship informed from the start.

## What to remember

Stablecoins improve one segment of a cross border payment: the movement of value between two points. They do not remove the need for conversion, compliance, controls or accounting. The businesses that benefit most will be those that treat them as one more payment rail, managed with the discipline they already apply to the others, and that measure success by what arrives, when, at what all in cost.

title: The Real Cost of an AI Agent
excerpt: The cost of an AI agent is rarely the model bill. Review time, integrations, evaluation and exceptions add up, and a business case that ignores them will not survive contact with real volume.
author: Altisly Strategy Team
content:
## The demo costs almost nothing

Every AI agent looks cheap in the first week. Someone wires a model to a few tools, points it at a support inbox or a reconciliation queue, and it works on the first twenty examples. The bill for that week is small enough to ignore, so the business case writes itself: look how little it costs, look how much time it saves.

Then the agent meets real volume, real mess and real accountability, and the cost curve stops resembling the demo. The model invoice is still there, but it is rarely the largest line. This piece is about the lines that tend to be missed.

## The model bill is the visible part

Start with the obvious cost, because it is easy to underestimate even that. An agent is not one model call. It is a loop: read the task, decide on a tool, call it, read the result, decide again. Each pass sends the growing conversation back to the model, so a task that takes eight steps costs far more than eight times a single call.

Three things drive this more than the choice of model:

- **Context length.** Long documents, full email threads and verbose tool outputs get re-read on every step. Trimming what the agent sees is usually the cheapest saving available.
- **Retries and dead ends.** An agent that wanders, calls the wrong tool and recovers is paying for the wandering. Tasks with a clear path cost less than open ended ones.
- **Model tier.** Using the most capable model for every step, including trivial ones like classifying a message, is a habit worth breaking. Many teams route simple steps to smaller models and keep the expensive one for judgement.

## The cost nobody budgets: checking the work

An agent that is right most of the time is not the same as an agent you can trust. The gap between those two is filled with people.

Someone has to review the outputs, at least at first. Someone has to read the cases where the agent was confidently wrong. Someone has to decide which categories of task are safe to run unattended and which always need a human to approve. This review work is real labour, and it does not disappear when the agent improves. It changes shape, from checking everything to sampling, and from sampling to investigating exceptions.

Picture a finance team that lets an agent draft vendor payment queries. If a wrong reply simply wastes a vendor's afternoon, light sampling is enough. If a wrong reply releases money, every output needs approval, and the time saved shrinks quickly. The same technology, with a very different cost profile, depending on what an error does.

So the first honest question in any agent business case is: what happens when it is wrong, and who catches it?

## Integration and upkeep

Agents act through tools, and tools are other people's systems. Each one is an integration that has to be built, secured, permissioned and maintained.

This is where agent projects quietly consume engineering time. An API changes a field name. A login method expires. A downstream system gets slow and the agent starts timing out mid task, leaving work half done. None of this is exotic, but all of it needs an owner.

Permissions deserve particular care. An agent that can read a ledger and also write to it carries a different risk from one that can only read. We prefer to give agents the narrowest access that lets them do the job, and to make every action they take leave a record a human can follow. That design work costs time up front and saves a great deal of argument later.

There is also the prompt and workflow itself. Instructions drift out of date as policies change. Edge cases accumulate. A system that nobody tunes slowly gets worse relative to the business around it, so budget for ongoing maintenance, not a one time build.

## Evaluation is a cost, and skipping it is a bigger one

You cannot improve what you cannot measure, and agents are hard to measure. The same input can produce different outputs. A change that helps one kind of task can quietly hurt another.

The fix is a test set: a collection of real, representative tasks with known good outcomes, that you run whenever you change the model, the prompt or a tool. Building it takes effort, because someone must collect the examples and agree what good looks like. But without it, every change is a gamble, and the team ends up afraid to touch a system that is supposedly saving them time.

Evaluation also gives you the number that matters most: how often the agent does the whole job correctly, end to end. Not how often it sounds plausible. That figure, measured on your own data, is the real basis for any decision about autonomy.

## Failure, exposure and the long tail

Some costs only show up on a bad day. An agent can be tricked by text hidden in a document it reads. It can make a confident mistake at volume, repeating it a few hundred times before anyone notices. It can expose information to a person who should not see it.

None of these are reasons to avoid agents. They are reasons to put limits around them: spending caps, rate limits, approval steps for irreversible actions, and a way to switch the whole thing off quickly. These controls are cheap to design in and expensive to retrofit after an incident.

## A better way to count

Instead of asking what the agent costs to run, ask what a completed task costs, end to end. Add model usage, review time, integration upkeep, evaluation effort and a sensible allowance for exceptions. Divide by the number of tasks done correctly, not the number attempted.

Compare that figure with what the same task costs today. Sometimes the agent wins easily. Sometimes the answer is that a plain script, or a better form, does the job for a tenth of the effort. Both are useful findings.

A good first move is to run the agent in shadow mode for a few weeks: let it do the work alongside your people, compare results, and record what it costs. You will have a real number by the end of it, which beats a hopeful one.
